news.title: US military says it fired on commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman after it attempted to breach blockade
news.text: EDNOTE: Adding inputs Jerusalem, Nov 8 (AP) US Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port. US forces have been enforcing a naval blockade on Iran for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial strategic waterway for shipping, including of oil. The last confirmed US strike on a cargo vessel was nearly a month ago in the Gulf of Oman. Saturday's disclosure comes in the wake of at least two instances in which US Central Command did not announce military strikes it has taken in the region and officials at the command declined to confirm strikes when asked about local reports of explosions. Iran state media also reported on Saturday evening the sound of explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several explosions in the port of Jask. It wasn't immediately clear what the cause of the explosions was and the US military didn't immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment. US President Donald Trump said Friday that the US military had carried out new limited strikes against Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system. Trump described the military action to reporters as “minor.” US Central Command ultimately didn't comment on the action even after the strikes were confirmed by Trump. For weeks now, Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections. The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the US resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months. (AP) ARB ARB

news.title: UFC boss says he will meet with Donald Trump over press secretary job offer
news.text:
Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White said he will fly to Washington to discuss President Donald Trump’s offer to become White House press secretary.

Mr Trump urged Mr White to take up the job in a Truth Social post on Saturday, naming several fighters from the mixed martial arts competition who could serve as assistants.

Speaking to reporters at an event in London, Mr White confirmed he would be meeting with the president.

“I have a meeting on Monday,” he said.

“I’m flying to DC right now and I’m sure we’ll have something to talk about after that.”

The president wrote on social media: “I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States.”

He added: “Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”

It remained unclear if the president’s offer was serious and the UFC boss would not be drawn on whether he would accept the role.

Mr White admitted he had “a lot of jobs already” and declined to divulge details of recent conversations with Mr Trump.

The position has remained vacant since mid-October after Katie Zacharia’s departure just five days into her tenure.

The appointment would follow a shake-up of the president’s team in the wake of heavy Republican losses in the midterm elections.

Republicans lost control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, as well as several key gubernatorial races.

Mr Trump also ousted his White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and replaced her with long-time aide Stephen Miller.

The White House press secretary effectively acts as the president’s chief spokesperson and deals with the media daily.

Mr Trump named six UFC fighters he wanted to see at the White House, including two born in Russia.

The president added: “I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris.

“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left.”

Mr White is a long-time ally of the president, speaking in support of him on the campaign trail and at the 2024 Republican National Convention.

The pair have frequently been spotted sitting ringside at UFC events.

In June, the fighting competition held an event on the White House south lawn to mark both America’s 250th independence celebrations and the president’s birthday.
news.summary: Dana White confirmed he would meet with the president on Monday.
news.author: Jessica Coates

news.title: MAGA voters reveal they broke ranks after ‘Trump put a target on America’s back’: NYT
news.text:
A key bloc of President Donald Trump's coalition broke toward Democrats in this week's midterms, and several told a reporter exactly why.

White voters without a college degree moved toward Democrats in Tuesday's elections, The New York Times reported Saturday. A majority still backed Republican House candidates, 59 percent to 40 percent, but that margin was 14 points narrower than Trump's 2024 edge with the group, according to the Times' voter analysis.

The group, which made up 39 percent of the electorate this year, has been central to Trump's coalition for more than a decade. In several key Senate contests, including Iowa's, the swing was even sharper.

Kylee Wilson, a 29-year-old bartender in Prairie City, Iowa, voted for Trump three times before backing Democrats this year. She told the Times the president had grown too combative and too entangled in the war with Iran while her family wrestled with rising costs and health care cuts.

"Trump put a target on America's back," Wilson said.

Alan Abramowitz, a political scientist at Emory University, told the Times that while many of these voters still oppose Democrats on abortion, LGBTQ rights and immigration, "people were really focused more on what was happening to their standard of living."

Kenneth Hessen, a 69-year-old retired truck driver, said at a Council Bluffs polling station that he had voted Republican since he was 18 but backed every Democrat on his ballot this year, angered by Medicaid cuts in Trump's tax and spending bill.

"If there was one under a rock, I'd vote for them today," he said.

Kevin Chadwick, who owns a towing and repair business in Harlan, Iowa, still supports Trump but voted for Democratic Senate nominee Josh Turek. He told the Times he was troubled that Republican nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson had grown millions of dollars richer in office, which Hinson has attributed to the sale of her husband's business.

Chadwick said the Democratic sweep "proves that money can't buy everything" after Elon Musk and other wealthy donors poured record sums into Republican campaigns.

Trump has blamed the Republican losses on not being on the ballot himself, an explanation other Republicans have rejected. Tim Charls, a longtime GOP voter who stuck with the party this year, wasn't buying it either.

"He's a drama queen," Charls said. "No, you lost. Like in 2020."

Republican strategist Alex Conant told the Times that working-class voters "thought Trump would fix the economy," but still see themselves slipping behind two years on.

Chadwick was uncertain his vote would change much. "I hope it gets better," he said. "But we hope that every election."

news.title: Why Delhi should take MP Ruhullah’s resignation as a loud warning from Kashmir
news.text:
Staying true to the promise he had made in September, Srinagar MP Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi resigned from the National Conference and the Lok Sabha on Tuesday.

“There are people who cry for the seat of power, but I feel at peace shunning the chair I am holding,” said 48-year-old Ruhullah as he announced his resignation at a massive gathering in Budgam. 

Ruhullah’s resignation was preceded by a biting speech that targeted Kashmir’s grand old party, the National Conference, and its two prominent faces, the father-son team of party President Farooq Abdullah and Chief Minister Omar Abdullah. With his resignation, Ruhullah – who is also a well-known religious figure – ended his nearly two-and-a-half-decade-long association with the party.

For many in Kashmir, the Shia cleric-politician’s resignation was not unexpected. It followed his growing isolation within the National Conference. He has been a vocal critic of the Bharatiya Janata Party-led Union government’s decision to scrap Jammu and Kashmir’s special status under the Constitution and statehood in August 2019. He has also been vociferous about his party’s refusal to make restoring these two items its primary agenda.

In 2024, in the run-up to the first Assembly elections in Jammu and Kashmir after it was downgraded to a Union Territory, the Abdullah-led National Conference pledged to restore the region’s special status if voted to power. In its manifesto for the polls, the party had also promised to “strive” to restore Article 370 and Article 35A – the two provisions that had guaranteed internal autonomy and protection in matters such as land and jobs for locals. These had also been annulled in August 2019.

While the National Conference achieved an overwhelming majority in the Assembly, many feel that the party, which has been in power for more than two years now, is not serious about taking on New Delhi over the question of restoring this special status. Ruhullah is more blunt. He claims that the National Conference has surrendered to the Bharatiya Janata Party.

Ruhullah’s rise has been fed by the growing displeasure towards the Omar Abdullah-led government in Kashmir. 

So far, the junior Abdullah has avoided taking a combative posture to the Union government’s writ in Kashmir. But to his credit, Abdullah has expressed his frustration with the current governance setup in Jammu and Kashmir several times.

However, many in Kashmir want him to do more, including giving up the chair if he has no power. Abdullah’s pragmatism is not only being viewed as surrender but increasingly even as collusion.

To the major issue of restoring Article 370 and Article 35A, the party has merely paid lip service. Also pending is the task of establishing the business rules that would delineate the role and functions of the elected government and the Lieutenant Governor-led administration in the Union Territory. 

While the final approval for those pending decisions remains with the unyielding Union government, Abdullah has been largely reticent in his response to the dominant Centre.

Ruhullah believes that the National Conference should make the restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s special status and autonomy its core agenda.

However, there is a constituency in Kashmir that is sceptical about Ruhullah’s exit: they believe it will further fragment the Kashmiri Muslim voter base. That scepticism springs from the history of New Delhi’s machinations in Kashmir. For decades, Union governments have created new political outfits in the Valley, broken up existing formations or backed obscure political outfits to cut powerful regional forces down to size.

This is why the biggest challenge for Ruhullah will be to convince Kashmiris that his politics is organic and does not have the blessings of the Union government. In his speech in Budgam on Tuesday, Ruhullah hinted at creating a new political formation. However, as a senior politician himself, Ruhullah, must know that there is a difference between platforming the grievances of Kashmir through speeches and turning a viewpoint into a powerful representative force. He faces an uphill task.

So far, the question Ruhullah has not answered is how he plans to compel New Delhi to restore the legal status quo in Kashmir. At the moment, the only difference between Omar Abdullah and Ruhullah is that Ruhullah has made the restoration of the special status of Jammu and Kashmir his core agenda.

Even though Ruhullah has been taking a strong line against the BJP-led Union government for nearly six years, he has failed to attract prominent voices or leaders to his side. But to his credit, a big chunk of Kashmiri youth do seem to like him.

At a deeper level, Ruhullah’s resignation is essentially a nudge to New Delhi to engage with Kashmir and address its anxieties. Whether the reason for these developments, New Delhi should read beyond Ruhullah’s resignation.

The massive support in his resignation rally in Budgam reiterated that there is support for the restoration of special status and autonomy of Jammu and Kashmir. New Delhi should not ignore the message.

Here is a summary of last week’s top stories.

A setback for Trump. The Democrats took control of the United States Congress from the Republicans in the mid-term elections. Before the polls, President Donald Trump-led Republican party had a 53-47 majority in the 100-member Senate. It had a slim 219-214 majority in the 435-member House of Representatives. 

As of 11 am Indian time on Saturday, the Democrats held 54 seats in the Senate and the Republicans had 44. In the House of Representatives, the Democrats had won 254 seats and the Republicans 162. Some seats were yet to be called. A party needs 218 seats for a majority in the Lower House.

The elections are being viewed as a verdict on Trump’s second term as president. The Democrats’ control of Congress is expected to lead to greater scrutiny of the Trump administration in the remaining two years of its tenure.

Counting in the elections to elect governors was also underway in 36 states and three territories. The Democrats won 22 gubernatorial posts where the polls were held and the Republicans 12.

Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate, won the gubernatorial election in Texas, a long-standing Republican stronghold. This is the first time the state will have a Democratic party governor in three decades.

Democratic leader Keisha Lance Bottoms won in Georgia, becoming the first Black woman to be elected as a governor of any state in the US. The party’s Abdul El‑Sayed won the Senate race in Michigan, becoming the first Muslim senator in the US.

India-born Nithya Raman won the Los Angeles mayoral election on a Democratic party ticket.

Vivek Ramaswamy loses, at least four Indian-Americans win, reports Oishika Neogi.

Agniveer extension. Seventy-five percent of Agniveers who are not enrolled in the armed forces permanently after their four-year tenure will be given an option to extend their service by two more years. After this six years of service, Agniveers will get another opportunity to join the armed forces as regular soldiers, provided they meet the criteria, said Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani.

The introduction of the short-service Agnipath scheme in June 2022 had triggered protests in several states as aspirants demanded permanent recruitment with pension benefits. The announcement on Wednesday came as around 18,000 Agniveers from the first batch are expected to complete their four-year tenure and exit in December.

Subramani said that Agniveers who opt for the additional two-year service will receive higher salaries and an increased exit package.

An Agniveer died in Operation Sindoor. A year later, his parents are still fighting for pension, reports Anant Gupta.

In court. The Bombay High Court said it was disturbed by remarks made by some politicians targeting actor Dia Mirza for a video she had shot on behalf of the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, urging Mumbai residents not to light firecrackers on the streets during Diwali. The court directed the municipal corporation to re-upload the video to “restore the confidence of the people”.

The municipal corporation had removed the video from its social media handles after the Bharatiya Janata Party’s city chief Ameet Satam declared, “We don’t need lessons on how to celebrate Diwali from Dia Mirza.”

The court said that the objections to Mirza’s participation in the civic body’s anti-pollution campaign were unfortunate and appeared to have given the matter a communal angle.

news.title: History Says Energy Led All Sectors in the Last Bear Market. Here's What's Different Now.
news.text:
Energy stocks were the clear winners during the 2022 bear market. The S&P 500 energy stocks delivered a total return of 65.7%, while the broader S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) lost 18.1%, including dividends.

Energy stocks are leading again in 2026, but without a broader bear market. S&P 500 energy stocks have gained 42% so far this year, compared with a 12% gain for the broader S&P 500 index, excluding dividends.

In 2022, rising oil prices boosted energy companies' earnings, while inflation and aggressive interest rate hikes weighed on the broader market. The 2026 rally has been supported by oil supply disruptions in the Middle East, with unusually high refining margins. But a recovery in global oil supplies could put pressure on energy profits and stock valuations.

Why energy's 2022 rally may not repeat

ExxonMobil (XOM +0.34%) reported earnings of $55.7 billion in 2022, compared with $23 billion in 2021. Chevron's (CVX -0.15%) earnings also more than doubled to $35.5 billion in 2022. Both companies returned billions to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

However, April 2025 offered a different picture. President Donald Trump's tariff announcements triggered a sharp market sell-off. The S&P 500 fell 21.3% from its February 2025 peak during intraday trading, but did not officially enter a bear market based on closing prices. But S&P 500 energy stocks fell 13.7% in April 2025, making energy the worst-performing sector.

Rising concerns about slowing economic growth and weaker oil demand negatively impacted energy stocks in April 2025. This also demonstrated that energy stocks do not outperform during every market downturn.

Global oil supplies may start rising

The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimated that 4.8 million barrels per day of Middle East crude oil production remained shut down in September 2026, compared with a peak of 10.9 million barrels per day in May. But damaged pipelines and risks to oil tankers continued to affect shipments.

However, EIA expects global liquid-fuels production to fall short of consumption by around 1.3 million barrels per day in 2026. The production is then projected to exceed consumption by approximately 5 million barrels per day in 2027. This represents a potential swing of nearly 6.3 million barrels per day in the global liquid-fuel supply-demand balance.

This forecast assumes that supply routes will reopen and production will also recover. If that happens, rising inventories could reduce oil prices even without a recession in the U.S. The EIA forecasts annual average Brent to decline from $96 per barrel in 2026 to $84 per barrel in 2027. However, renewed geopolitical tensions or slower infrastructure repairs could delay the recovery.

Oil markets are already responding to expectations of easing supply disruptions. Brent crude prices dropped below $100 this week. Hopes of peace agreements involving Iran and Ukraine contributed to the decline, even though the underlying supply disruptions had not been fully resolved. 

Why energy companies' record profits may not last

In the third quarter of 2026, ExxonMobil's Energy Products segment, which includes refining and fuels, reported earnings close to $7.2 billion. Chevron's downstream business earnings also more than quadrupled to $4.9 billion in the third quarter of 2026.

However, these strong downstream earnings may not persist. Disruptions to refineries in the Middle East and Russia have constrained gasoline and diesel supplies. This has pushed their selling prices higher relative to crude oil. However, as damaged refineries resume production and fuel supplies recover, the difference between refined product and crude oil prices could narrow.

Lower crude prices could also hurt earnings from oil production. ExxonMobil estimates that every $1 per barrel change in Brent crude prices would affect its annual upstream after-tax earnings by approximately $700 million, based on expected 2026 operations. Applying this sensitivity to the EIA's projected $12-per-barrel decline in annual average Brent crude oil prices suggests a potential $8.4 billion annual headwind for Exxon's upstream earnings. This estimate assumes that Exxon's production volumes, costs, and other operating conditions remain largely unchanged.

Are energy stocks worth buying now?

According to FactSet Research Systems' Oct. 30 report, S&P 500 energy stocks traded at 13.2 times expected earnings over the next 12 months, significantly lower than S&P 500's forward 12-month price-to-earnings ratio of 18.7x. However, the valuation of S&P 500 energy stocks was above its own five-year average forward 12-month PE of 12.6.

According to analyst estimates compiled by FactSet, S&P 500 energy sector earnings are expected to decline 7.8% in 2027, compared with projected earnings growth of 16.3% for the broader S&P 500. This suggests that energy's lower valuation relative to the broader market may reflect expectations of weaker future earnings, rather than necessarily making the sector a bargain.

I would avoid aggressively buying energy stocks after their substantial gains in 2026. A recovery in oil supplies could weaken earnings, even if the broader stock market remains strong.
news.summary: Energy stocks have delivered exceptional gains in 2026, but a surprising shift in the oil market could change the outlook for investors.

news.title: Trump confirms fresh US strikes on Iranian air defences amid talks with Tehran
news.text: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump has confirmed that American forces carried out fresh strikes on Iranian air defence systems on Qeshm Island, even as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict continue.Trump described the operation as a minor strike, saying US forces had destroyed an anti-aircraft system that Iran had recently built. He made the remarks to reporters on Friday while travelling to Florida.The strikes came after attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that at least 11 ships had been targeted in the area over the past week, with three sinking.Despite the military escalation, Washington and Tehran have continued discussions through regional mediators. Qatar has been involved in efforts to broker an understanding that could include the US lifting its blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and releasing some frozen Iranian assets. In return, Iran could allow International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to visit nuclear sites damaged in earlier strikes.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he had spoken with several foreign ministers in an effort to prevent further escalation. Qatar’s Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani also said mediation between the two sides remained active.The US has meanwhile announced the creation of a new task force to prevent Iran from moving weapons and other restricted materials through land routes and the Caspian Sea.The latest strikes underscore the uncertainty surrounding the conflict, with military action continuing alongside negotiations. Trump has said Tehran wants a deal, but no agreement has been announced.With input from media reports.

news.title: Judge wants former US attorney to investigate whether the government misled her in Trump golf case
news.text: WASHINGTON — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation's capital during President Donald Trump's first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River.Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers.The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a 'World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events.' An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and the administration must give 10 days' notice in writing before making any 'irreparable modification' to any 'forms or features' of the course while the lawsuit is active.Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled.Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government's conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys.As the city's chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump's 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking Justice Department job.Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee because of her past membership in a lawyers' group that has supported abortion rights. She eventually resigned from the group because, she said previously, it took left-leaning positions, and she is now part of her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP.David Super, a law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, said the initiation of a formal investigation by a judge to look into the conduct of a trial's participants 'can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court.'Super said it also is a reflection 'of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn't have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues.'Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on.The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when administration officials could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Oct. 28 that the plans were real.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: Trump, 80, Instantly Flunks Kindergarten-Level Civility Test
news.text:
In his first one-on-one interview since the midterms, President Donald Trump promised to be more civil toward his political opponents—but couldn’t resist trotting out his favorite insult for Democrats.

Trump sat down with 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat for an interview at the White House Friday and was asked if he could work with Democrats without insulting them.

“Do you think you could work with the Democrats without insulting them, consistently?” Douthat asked.

“Yeah, I do. I could... I also called many of them ‘Dumocrats,’” Trump replied, unnecessarily reminding the journalist—and viewers—of the insult. 

Douthat pressed him: “You did that just the other day. If it took six months of not insulting the Democrats to get a deal done, do you think you could do it?”

Trump insisted he could. “Very easily.”

The clip also addressed Trump calling Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico “Talafreako” repeatedly during the campaign, which Trump acknowledged—but did not apologize for.

CBS released the excerpt as a teaser ahead of Sunday night’s broadcast.

The sit-down is a coup for the beleaguered 60 Minutes, which has been rocked by dismal ratings since its return in October.

After CBS was acquired by Trump-friendly nepo baby David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance in 2025, the network has been pushed in a MAGA-friendly direction.

In October 2025, Ellison appointed Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief of CBS News, despite her having no broadcast news experience. 

In spring 2026, Weiss made sweeping changes at 60 Minutes, the network’s flagship current affairs program.

She axed veteran correspondents and producers and installed a new executive producer, Nick Bilton, who, like Weiss, was a television greenhorn.

Respected veteran correspondent Scott Pelley was fired after a heated confrontation with Bilton.

Douthat, a conservative journalist, was hired in July from The New York Times and was tapped for the Trump interview over veteran correspondents including Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, Jon Wertheim, and Norah O’Donnell.

Stahl, 84, who received the inaugural Daily Beast Power 100 Award on Thursday, said during a speech at the awards luncheon that she considered leaving the program during Weiss’ spring purge. Ultimately, fearing the legendary program would be killed altogether—and hoping to protect her remaining colleagues’ jobs—she opted to stay.

Weiss accompanied Douthat to the White House. 

The choice to sit down with a MAGA-friendly journalist is not surprising, given Trump’s naked hostility toward the media in the run-up to the midterms.

The president banned CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from the White House amid mounting frustration over a series of polls and stories he disliked.

Branding them “fake news,” he argued that reporters should report good news about him.

Even though the ban was reversed by the courts on First Amendment grounds, Trump has continued to label media outlets and individual journalists as “fake” when he doesn’t like their reporting. 

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump sat down with 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat for an interview at the White House Friday and was asked if he could work with Democrats without insulting them.

news.title: Trump’s choice
news.text:
ALTHOUGH American President Donald Trump has admitted that the disastrous Iran war was a factor in the heavy drubbing his party received from the Democrats in the midterm polls, there are few indications he has decided to wind down the conflict. In fact, Mr Trump has sent mixed messages, saying there has been “progress” in talks with Iran, while also threatening to “destroy what is left” of the Islamic Republic should negotiations fail.

These are hardly reassuring words for the international community, which wants the war to end quickly. Qatar has taken centre stage in mediation, with Mr Trump discussing the Iran file with the country’s emir.

There is genuine reason to fear another US strike on Iran. For one, Mr Trump may want to act before January 2027, when the new Congress is empowered to scrutinise his decisions.

The US government on Saturday asked its citizens in the Middle East to “exercise heightened vigilance”, while it has struck the Iranian island of Qeshm twice this week. The Iranians have not taken the bait, but have promised strong retaliation to new attacks.

These developments illustrate the unpredictability of the Gulf situation: one rash move could restart the conflict, which is why mediation efforts should be stepped up.

The US leadership is mistaken if it thinks that a fresh round of hostilities would be ‘limited’. If Iran does retaliate to new American or Israeli strikes, the impact of the conflict could be far more devastating than the last round. Along with needless aggression against a sovereign state, the economic shockwave caused by the conflict would hit ordinary people everywhere.

In order to prevent a new military and economic crisis, the US leadership must prioritise diplomacy over war. The Iranians want an end to the blockade of their ports, as well as lifting of sanctions and the release of their funds. All these are achievable goals if the US sincerely desires peace. Even the nuclear issue can be resolved at the negotiating table if Mr Trump eschews his threatening tone.

In return, Iran should promise unhindered navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. Moreover, the ceasefire must be broadened to stop the Yemen conflict as well as Israeli violence in Lebanon and the occupied Palestinian territories. Though technically, these are separate conflicts, they are also interlinked, involving Iran’s allies in the ‘Axis of Resistance’.

It is decision time for Mr Trump. He can either work with regional states and negotiate an end to his own ‘forever war’. Or he can continue down the same path, with the international community paying the price for American and Israeli bellicosity. For the sake of peace, it is hoped he chooses the former option.

Published in Dawn, November 8th, 2026

news.title: Jaws drop as ‘wrong Dana White’ theory swirls around Trump’s ‘bizarrely stupid’ move
news.text:
A wild theory about President Donald Trump's latest pick for a top White House job left jaws on the floor.

Trump announced Saturday on Truth Social that he had offered the press secretary job to UFC boss Dana White, hailing him as "a violent Fighter and Warrior." Within hours, observers were floating a stunning possibility.

Online commentators suggested that someone may have recommended a different Dana White, a former Pentagon spokesperson from Trump's first term, and the president grabbed the wrong one.

The offer itself is real. According to CNN, a source said White turned the job down. Trump's last press secretary, Katie Zacharia, left in October after only five days.

Nothing suggests the mix-up theory has been confirmed. But that didn't stop it from racing across X.

"So what are the chances someone suggested this Dana White and Trump pulled a Four Seasons Total Landscaping?" asked Connor Ewing, a political science professor at the University of Toronto, referring to the infamous 2020 press conference Rudy Giuliani held outside a Philadelphia landscaping company instead of the luxury hotel. Ewing's post had about 1.1 million views as people chimed in on the theory.

"The fact that there is a nonzero chance that this happened..." mused the progressive news network MeidasTouch.

Veteran NFL writer Doug Farrar pointed out that the timing made it even better, since Saturday marked the anniversary of Giuliani's landscaping debacle.

"So, here’s what likely happened. Someone suggested Dana W. White (who is a Trumpublican) to him, and he got it wrong," Farrar wrote. "That’s not the best part. The best part is that this happened on the anniversary of Four Seasons Total Landscaping."

George Conway, the conservative attorney turned fierce Trump critic, called the scenario "so insanely and completely bizarrely stupid that you know this is exactly what must have happened."

Other conservative commentators weren't ruling it out either.

"No idea if this happened," said Jonah Goldberg, editor-in-chief of the right-leaning outlet The Dispatch. "But literally no one can plausibly claim the chances of this being true aren't greater than zero."

"This theory seems crazy," added conservative columnist Matt Lewis. "But NOT as crazy as making the UFC guy your WH press secretary."

Award-winning Christian novelist Jennifer Erin Valent warned that "this is actually possible. And that should frighten us all."

Democratic influencer Harry Sisson ticked through Trump's chaotic week, noting "it's been revealed it's likely the wrong Dana White," before concluding that Trump is "falling apart."

Nebraska progressive activist and Karoline Leavitt foe Jamie Bonkiewicz fired off the sharpest jab of the bunch.

“Someone said ‘Dana White for press secretary’ and meant the former Pentagon spokesperson. Trump heard ‘the UFC guy’ and went with it,” she quipped. “And we’re expected to believe this dumb motherf— aced three cognitive tests?”

news.title: Judiciary Must Protect This Democracy
news.text:
When news broke on Thursday that Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court had sacked the David Mark-led caretaker committee of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and consequently nullified the nomination of Alhaji Atiku Abubakar as the party’s presidential candidate, my initial response was: are we still on this matter? Maybe I slept off along the way. All I had on my mind was that we were now fully set for the epic 2027 presidential election without further drama. I was already doing my permutations on a three-horse race, silently praying for a free and fair process so that we can have something more to celebrate in our democratic journey. My spirit was dampened once again.

The judgment, which the ADC said it has appealed, declared the party’s caretaker committee illegal in the suit brought by Alhaji Nafiu Bala Gombe, the former national deputy chairman (north-east) of the party. The judge also invalidated all decisions taken by the committee. In simplified language, all the primaries conducted by the committee are null and void. That means the party does not have a presidential candidate, much less flagbearers for the governorship and legislative elections. Basically, the ADC, as things stand, will not participate in the 2027 general election. Lifu decided that all the actions taken by the Mark-led committee are illegal, null, void and of no effect. That is massive!

The ADC immediately blamed the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) for the judgment. In a statement, Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, the ADC spokesperson, described the verdict as a “desperate attempt to cripple the opposition and deny Nigerians the right to choose their leaders in the forthcoming general elections”. He said the judgment’s timing, barely 24 hours after the “massive turnout” at the ADC presidential campaign rally in Sokoto, “exposes the growing desperation of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC)”. Atiku, for his part, said “it is part of a strategy to weaken my support in the north and frustrate a campaign whose message is resonating across the country”.

The APC rejected the ADC allegation. Olorogun Festus Keyamo, the minister of aviation and aerospace development, also issued a strongly-worded statement. “Justice may be slow, but it is always SURE!” Keyamo wrote on X. “You cannot invade a political Party owned and built by Nigerians, hijack it with the connivance of a so-called National Chairman without a PRIOR meeting and approval of a mini National Convention or the National Executive Committee and hope to bluff your way out of such a brazen act by blaming and blackmailing the ruling Party for a misfortune deliberately stoked by you. Sorry, but the law is decided on facts and evidence, rather than sentiments and outrage…”

For those who may be late to the party, trouble started when some opposition politicians joined the ADC last year. Its national officers, led by Chief Ralph Nwosu, resigned. Mark became the chairman of the caretaker committee and Ogbeni Rauf Aregbesola the national secretary in July 2025. Two months later, Gombe filed an ex parte motion before Justice Emeka Nwite of the Federal High Court, saying he did not resign and asking that he be declared the authentic acting chairman following Nwosu’s resignation. He asked the court to stop the committee from “parading” themselves as national officers. The court did not grant the ex parte motion but asked Mark to file a defence.

However, Mark proceeded to the Court of Appeal to challenge the jurisdiction of the high court since the Supreme Court had ruled that a party’s internal affairs should not be determined by a court. Mark also appealed the order directing him to file a defence. The Court of Appeal told Mark that since the matter was still “live” at the high court, he needed leave of the same court to file an appeal, but Mark argued that it was a fundamental right and leave was not needed. Still, the appeal court dismissed the appeal, describing it as premature. The “status quo ante bellum” should be maintained, it further ruled. We started arguing over the meaning of “status quo ante bellum”.

Dissatisfied with the ruling by the Court of Appeal, Mark headed for the Supreme Court. He made the same argument: that the high court had no jurisdiction and that it ought not to have entertained Gombe’s interlocutory application. The apex court partly repeated what the appeal court said: that the matter was still “live” at the high court and Mark needed to seek leave of that court to file an appeal. What was the appeal exactly? The high court had yet to determine the substantive issues before it, so an appeal was not the appropriate course of action. Therefore, the high court must first rule on whether or not it has jurisdiction before Mark could file the kind of appeal he was pursuing.

After the Supreme Court verdict, Gombe’s lawyers asked for the case to be moved away from Nwite but Mark’s lawyers opposed the request, calling it “forum shopping”. In the meantime, Nwite was promoted to the Court of Appeal, and Lifu, whom the ADC did not fancy because of a previous adverse judgment against the party, was assigned to the case. Aregbesola filed a motion asking Lifu to step aside. So did the party’s welfare secretary, Nkemakolam Ukandu. Lifu dismissed the request. Ukandu also sued the National Judicial Council (NJC) and Justices John Tsoho and Lifu. The court struck out the suit and asked him to pay N50 million each to Tsoho and Lifu for failing to pursue it.

Where do I stand on this burning issue? The first thing I want to do is to implore the judiciary to tread carefully. Political tension is already rising ahead of the 2027 general election. Our judges must do everything possible and reasonable to avoid compounding the situation. They must not become part of the problem. The judges must act with restraint and a sense of responsibility in order protect this democracy. I am particularly worried that courts of equal jurisdiction are making contradictory pronouncements on similar cases. Something is terribly wrong and this has to stop. Am I suggesting that because a case is political, the judges should ignore the facts of the matter? No. Not exactly.

While I suspect that the way and manner Atiku and his allies took over the ADC left much to be desired, I am also of the opinion that you cannot abort a child that has been born, as Bashorun MKO Abiola would say. I am a journalist. I am not a lawyer. But I would argue that the Mark-led committee had been functioning with judicial backing. Indeed, on July 2, 2026, Justice Musa Liman of the Federal High Court upheld the emergence of Mark and Aregbesola as ADC leaders in a separate suit filed by Hon. Leke Abejide. He held that it complied with the party’s constitution and the electoral law. The party, therefore, was not acting without legal cover when it conducted the primaries.

The judges, I would add, must seriously consider the question of whether the injury allegedly suffered by Gombe can be remedied without invalidating every decision taken by the party and potentially disenfranchising millions of Nigerians who would ordinarily have the ADC as one of their electoral choices. That is a question worth examining within the limits of the law. As a layman (and I am ready to defer to superior argument), I do not think nullifying every action and every decision of the caretaker committee is the best way to give justice to Gombe, even if that was his prayer before the high court. His grievance can still be addressed through a pragmatic judicial pronouncement.

It is not my place to prescribe to the judges how they should do their job. That is above my pay grade. But I have a fundamental right to air my opinion on matters of national interest. Thus, it should go without saying that this case has to be disposed of quickly. This is what the National Assembly would call “a matter of urgent national importance”. Elections are just 10 weeks away. We do not have the luxury of time. The ADC contributed to the delay by prolonging the litigation through interlocutory appeals instead of allowing the high court to determine the substantive matter earlier. The ADC contributed to the delay by not allowing the high court to rule on the substantive matter.

The judiciary must uphold the law, but justice is not always served by adopting the most destructive remedy available. Where the law permits, courts should consider whether a remedy can address an established wrong without pointlessly undermining the rights of innocent parties and the electorate. To be clear, I am not suggesting that the judiciary should legitimise illegality or shield politicians from the consequences of their actions. That would be another way of undermining democracy. Rather, my appeal is that, in dispensing justice, our courts must also ensure that the remedy does not create a greater problem than the wrong it seeks to correct. Not everything that is lawful is expedient.

AND FOUR OTHER THINGS…

ATIKU OR OBI?

My assumption all along is that if Mr Peter Obi had not left the ADC, the party would have had a very strong chance of unseating President Bola Tinubu in 2027. Splitting the opposition into two would only empower the APC, I argued. Hypothetically, if Alhaji Atiku Abubakar is eventually disqualified from the 2027 presidential race, as a Federal High Court has done pending appeal, will this benefit Obi, candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC)? For one, it will be an all-south affair and fears of the disruption of the power rotation understanding will be allayed. But I am unsure if Atiku’s supporters are transferable to Obi. There may be a recalibration along our other fault lines. Dicey.

SANUSI’S SHOT

Alhaji Muhammadu Sanusi II, emir of Kano, has said President Tinubu deserves credit for bringing Nigeria’s economy back from the brink. He made specific reference to improvements in economic growth, the inflation rate, foreign reserves, and export diversification. “I’m not a fan of politicians, but we need to give credit to President Tinubu’s administration for bringing us back from the brink,” he said at an Oxford Global Think Tank conference. But he said something that Tinubu needs to seriously chew upon: “This government doesn’t express itself properly. It sees every suggestion and contribution it does not like as an attack, and it doesn’t have good spokespersons.” Exactly.

DOWN, NOT OUT

President Donald Trump was taught a political lesson by American voters in the midterm elections on Tuesday, with his Republican Party losing control of the Senate and the House of Representatives to the Democratic Party. It was mostly down to his meaningless and thoughtless war with Iran — which instigated energy inflation across the world and caused a cost of living crisis for billions, including Nigerians. But those who know Trump will not underrate the damage he can still cause in the remaining two years of his presidency. He can keep waging war against America’s friends and foes and use his veto to stall bills passed by the Congress. It is not yet Uhuru. After all, it is Trump. Erratic.

Senator Tahir Monguno, senate chief whip and senator representing Borno north, raised a motion on Tuesday seeking a review and enforcement of Nigeria’s bilateral air services agreement (BASA) with China to allow Nigerian airlines to operate direct flights to the Asian country. But it was something else that was troubling Senate President Godswill Akpabio: scarcity of private jets for campaigns. “Watch December and the confusion. Even the private airlines cannot handle. Common campaigns, we cannot see even private jets to hire,” said Akpabio, who makes an average of one outrageous statement per day. Meanwhile, poor Nigerians are busy crying over the price of garri. Wonderful.

news.title: US Midterm Elections and the Rest of Us
news.text:
Postscript by Waziri Adio

US elections have had a global following for a while. But it is doubtful if any other American election, including presidential polls, has been more keenly watched across the globe than the midterm elections of November 3rd, 2026. The reason is simple. The US, in the second coming of President Donald Trump, has become a major source of global anxiety. On Tuesday, the American electorate handed Mr. Trump and his Republican Party a stinging rebuke, to the obvious relief of many across the world who expect this domestic chastening to mark a positive shift in America’s global engagement. They may be right, and they may not be.

It must be emphasised that American voters, including some of the tribally partisan ones, decided to punish a president who was elected just two years ago on the promise of making life more affordable for Americans but who seemed bent on doing the opposite. It must also be noted that most American voters in the midterm elections were preoccupied with local issues, not global ones. But Trump managed to connect the global to the local in the place where Americans are most sensitive: their pockets and their dining tables. With the strong message from the voters and with the Democratic Party taking control of Congress in January, Trump is expected to dial back some of the actions fuelling high prices, and reinvigorated institutions of restraint are likely to provide much-needed checks.

The most obvious point of relief for Americans and non-Americans alike is the likely end of the US-Israeli war on Iran and of Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The Trump-induced crisis in the Middle East constrained the global supply of oil and gas (and fertiliser), and created an energy crisis that put the world at risk and from which US consumers are not insulated. On account of the war and its aftermath, the average price of petrol in the US went from $2.91 per gallon to $4.40, while the average price of diesel jumped from $3.72 per gallon to $6— increases of 51% and 61% respectively within just nine months. Needless to say, this has had implications for the cost of energy and groceries, and Americans did not find it funny. Beyond America’s shores, Trump’s war of choice has increased the risk of another global recession, inflicted pain on consumers across the globe and put governments in different countries under intense pressure.

“The reason we lost is the (Iran) war,” Vice President JD Vance posted on social media the day after American voters delivered their unmistakable verdict. “The president himself said so last night.” The energy markets reacted positively to the outcome of the polls and to Vance’s blunt assessment. The price of a barrel of Brent crude fell from $110.45 at the beginning of the week to $98.32 on Friday, an 11% drop within the week. The expectation of the markets, of Americans and of the rest of the world is that Trump will quickly focus on ending the war with Iran. If this happens, the prices of crude oil and refined products such as petrol, diesel and aviation fuel are expected to fall even further.

The de-escalation will be needed primarily to appease Americans. But the benefits will not be confined to them, just as the consequences of the war have not been restricted to them. The impact of this avoidable energy crisis is being felt across the globe. In Nigeria, the prices of petrol and diesel rose by 40-90% within nine months, with direct effects on transport, food and energy costs for individuals and on operating costs for businesses. This is significant for a country where most citizens are yet to fully adjust to the shocks of petrol subsidy removal and the devaluation of the national currency. If crude prices fall back to $65-75 per barrel, they will still be above the $64.85 oil price benchmark used in Nigeria’s 2026 budget, and they should bring the price of petrol below N1,000 per litre in the country. This will be a big relief for businesses, households and even the Nigerian government, and it is likely to reduce the appeal of the fiscally reckless but populist promise by some presidential candidates to restore petrol subsidy. In that wise, the local decision made by American voters on November 3rd is likely to benefit Nigerians and consumers in different corners of the globe who are reeling from an avoidable global energy crisis.

In addition to ending the war with Iran, Trump may also, in a bid to address high domestic prices, scale back his indiscriminate imposition of tariffs on imports into the US. Trump has operated under the mistaken belief that any country with a trade surplus with the US must be cheating America, and that tariffs would be borne by exporters. However, it is now and always obvious that tariffs are taxes on consumers. Even though exporters may suffer from reduced demand and income, the real losers are the end consumers. Trump’s tariff wars, clothed in nationalistic garb, have imposed a high cost on America and on other countries, some of which have had to impose retaliatory tariffs.

The tariffs have been challenged in US courts, with the US Supreme Court ruling in February this year that Trump exceeded his executive authority in imposing sweeping tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). The administration has since been exploring other statutes to advance Trump’s preferred trade tool. The feedback from the voters may rein in Trump’s appetite for tariffs. But the impact here may not be as consequential or as universal for the rest of the world as ending the war with Iran, since different countries are affected differently by Trump’s tariff wars.

It is important not to read the outcome of the US midterms as a reprimand of America’s interventions in other countries or as a disapproval of Trump’s gruff treatment of American allies and international institutions. As noted earlier, the voters were preoccupied with local issues on November 3rd. Global affairs and foreign policy barely registered during the campaigns or as priorities for voters, perhaps understandably. Even though Americans say they are tired of forever wars, they did not disapprove of Trump’s invasion of Venezuela and are unlikely to bat an eyelid if he decides to invade Cuba next. The only reason they are bothered about the war in Iran is that it made gasoline, groceries and other necessities less affordable for them.

Similarly, while a majority of Americans may not endorse Trump’s hostility towards the United Nations, the International Criminal Court (ICC), Europe and Canada, or his cosiness with Vladimir Putin and other strongmen, those were not the reasons they voted against him and his party on Tuesday. It would be wrong to expect Trump to change his attitude and ways in these areas, precisely because he has no incentive to do so and is unlikely to come under any pressure to. The Democrats in Congress will definitely hold him to account and keep him in check. But they are more likely to focus on domestic issues, and only on those global issues that have a direct domestic impact (like putting America first). Leading members of the Republican Party, including those in Trump’s cabinet, are likely to break ranks with him as they prepare for a post-Trump future. Some of them may occasionally join forces with the Democrats, but likely only on domestic issues with electoral consequences.

One way Trump may respond to his humiliation at home may be to look for those to safely humiliate abroad, and that could include America’s traditional allies. At home, Trump has surely begun his lame-duck phase. But as America’s president for the next two years, he can still do a lot of damage abroad. Besides, those who see the outcome of November 3rd as a possible turning point in how America engages the world may be getting a bit too excited. There is no guarantee that the next American president, even if a Democrat, will depart from the path America has firmly embraced: growing insularity and the weaponisation of dependency. That is a space to watch. The need for a concert of middle powers to rethink and reinvent the global order has not been overtaken by events. The post-WW2 global order was built around undue dependence on America. It should be clear to all by now that this cannot endure forever.

However, one lesson of the midterms that is not discussed enough is that the idea of America as a beacon of light is still very much alive. Within two years of Trump 2.0, America had started looking more like a country firmly under the thumb of one man and less like the greatest democratic experiment of the modern world. To be sure, it will take more than one election to know if some irreparable damage has not been done, but these elections have shown that reports of the death of democracy in America have been somewhat exaggerated.

The voters have shown the way. The culture that underpins democracy has not given way. Some of the vital institutions have held firm. The outcome of the election, with many firsts, is a better reflection of the diversity of America. The mechanisms for restraint and accountability are likely to be re-energised. For the global community that needs the US to continue to be the shining city on a hill, a positive example of democratic ethos and practice, November 3rd is a cheery even if cautious affirmation.

news.title: UFC boss says he will meet with Donald Trump over press secretary job offer
news.text:
Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White said he will fly to Washington to discuss President Donald Trump’s offer to become White House press secretary.

Mr Trump urged Mr White to take up the job in a Truth Social post on Saturday, suggesting he bring several current and past fighters from the mixed martial arts competition to serve as assistants.

Speaking to reporters at an event in London, Mr White confirmed he would be meeting with the president.

“I have a meeting on Monday,” he said.

“I’m flying to DC right now and I’m sure we’ll have something to talk about after that.”

The president wrote on social media: “I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States.”

He added: “Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”

The UFC boss has not said whether he will accept the role, which has sat vacant since October when Katie Zacharia left after less than a week in the job.

news.title: Washington takes Tehran pressure campaign ashore
news.text:
Centcom forms ‘Task Force Iron Gate’ to choke Iran’s land, Caspian supply routes; Adm Cooper says force is an internal unit rather than a military deployment; Pakistan among four Iran neighbours listed on command’s graphic• Qatar PM warns against new escalation, urges ‘good deal’ over ‘perfect’ one• Iran claims military ‘stronger than at start of war’, vows ‘immediate’ response to attack

WASHINGTON: The United States is expanding its campaign against Iran’s military supply chains and revenue sources beyond the sea, with US Central Command (Centcom) announcing a task force on Saturday to disrupt the flow of advanced weapons and other materials through land routes.

Centcom commander Admiral Brad Cooper directed the creation of Task Force Iron Gate, an internal team of about 20 civilian and military personnel based in Tampa, Florida.

The team will coordinate with other US government agencies to monitor and disrupt the movement of advanced weapons, sensitive technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Centcom said the task force will focus on advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams. An accompanying graphic described its mission as “monitor, detect and disrupt” illicit movements.

“The establishment of Task Force Iron Gate reinforces the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea,” Cooper said.

“Strengthening Centcom’s collaboration with US interagency partners will further constrain Iran’s ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories and replenish their military.”

Centcom said the US naval blockade had prevented Iran from exporting more than $25 billion worth of crude oil in recent months. The new task force is intended to target alternative supply and commercial networks that could help Iran circumvent maritime restrictions.

The Caspian Sea connects Iran with Russia and countries in Central Asia and the Caucasus.

A Centcom graphic specifically highlights Iran’s borders with Turkiye, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan and Pakistan, which shares an approximately 900-kilometre border and commercial road connections with Iran, though the command described an internal team rather than a new military deployment and announced no agreement with Islamabad.

The announcement followed a Treasury Department move to designate eight digital asset service providers accused of helping Iran’s government, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other sanctioned actors move money through cryptocurrencies.

Washington also offered a reward of up to $20 million, along with possible relocation, for information about Iran’s nuclear programme. The State Dep-artment’s Rewards for Justice programme is seeking information about nuclear facilities, equipment and associated personnel, including scientists.

Diplomatic efforts

As Washington widens its pressure, mediators including Qatar were trying to prevent the conflict from spiralling out of control.

Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani warned that the Iran issue cannot be left unresolved and the region cannot afford another round of escalation, Al Jazeera TV reported.

Al Thani said the US administration remained willing to find a solution after Tuesday’s midterm elections, signalling Washington’s interest in an agreement had not changed.

After US President Donald Trump called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani on Friday to discuss ending the war, the prime minister applauded US colleagues for “genuine intentions to find a way to contain the situation and to de-escalate it”.

“Thanks also to some wise voices in Tehran, we have prevented that from getting out of control,” Al Thani said in Oxford on Friday, expressing confidence a settlement could be reached after significant progress.

“We cannot wait to reach a perfect agreement; we hope to reach a good agreement,” he said, urging priority for the nuclear issue, freedom of navigation and Gulf security.

Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on Instagram that he had held telephone calls with ministers from 12 countries over the previous 48 hours.

Iran’s prepared

The diplomatic push comes as Tehran signals it is prepared for further confrontation as Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said on Saturday that their military had grown “stronger” since the outset of the war.

Akraminia told state news agency IRNA that Iran’s forces “are on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war”.

“They now possess greater motivation, commitment and self-confidence,” Akraminia added. “Under the order of the Supreme Leader, the response of the armed forces will be immediate, effective and without geographical limitations.”

Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told Fars news agency that “the increase in the range of Iran’s missiles continues steadily” without pause.

Meanwhile, Akraminia said the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries one-fifth of global oil consumption, would remain closed until Washington meets Tehran’s demands under a seven-day plan proposed in September — and rejected by Trump — to lift the blockade of Iranian ports, unfreeze assets and approve an Iranian-backed route.

Tensions around the Strait of Hormuz have added to the uncertainty. On Saturday, Iran’s army said a tanker in the strait “caught fire and came to a halt after striking a naval mine”, despite recent US assertions that all mines were cleared.

Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency also reported two missiles struck Qeshm Island in the strait, while state media said air defences “struck and destroyed” a US drone overhead.

Although regional countries anticipated Trump might resume attacks after Tuesday’s midterms, where Republicans suffered heavy losses, the US has announced no new strikes inside Iran.

Trump said that eight months of war had severely damaged Iran’s economy and military and obliterated its nuclear programme.

“We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly,” Trump said, though International Crisis Group analyst Ali Vaez warned “a lame duck Trump could become a flame duck if Iran denies him a face-saving exit”.

news.title: Amaechi: Buhari Promised Me APC Presidential Ticket in 2022
news.text:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja

The African Democratic Congress (ADC) vice-presidential candidate, Mr Rotimi Amaechi, has blamed his defeat in the 2022 All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential primary on his decision to follow the advice of the late President Muhammadu Buhari not to campaign ahead of the contest.

Amaechi said Buhari had assured him in writing that he would announce him as his preferred candidate, prompting him to refrain from lobbying delegates and negotiating political alliances ahead of the primary.

He disclosed this during an interview on Mainland 98.3FM’s The Situation Room programme in Lagos on Friday, while reflecting on how President Bola Tinubu defeated him to clinch the APC presidential ticket in 2022.

According to Amaechi, he considered Buhari’s position credible because the former president was his boss and believed his endorsement would give him an advantage over other aspirants.

He said, “The first mistake that I made at that primary was that I listened to President Buhari. He said to me, ‘don’t campaign, don’t do anything, I will announce you as my candidate.’

“He told me that. He put it in writing. When I write my book, I’ll put it out.”

The former Minister of Transportation said his decision not to negotiate political positions with governors and other influential party members also worked against his ambition, and gave Tinubu an opportunity to build alliances ahead of the primary.

Amaechi explained that he could have secured the support of governors by promising them political appointments, including the positions of vice-president and Secretary to the Government of the Federation.

 “Now, I didn’t do deals. So, I would have promised you vice-president, promised you SGF, and then would have gone for this primary, I would have possibly won. I would have had governors on my side.

“Because I didn’t do deals, Tinubu had the chance to do deals,” he said.

Amaechi, who was also a presidential aspirant in the 2022 APC primary, further accused Tinubu of exploiting religious sentiments to secure support from delegates, particularly in the North.

He, however, said he would not deploy religion as a political tool to win elections, describing his position as a reflection of his nationalist convictions.

The ADC chieftain alleged that a delegation of Southern Yoruba Muslims had approached governors in the North-West and appealed to them to support Tinubu on religious grounds.

He also cited the position of former Kaduna State Governor Nasir El-Rufai, whom he said had supported his presidential ambition before eventually backing Tinubu.

 “El-Rufai was my supporter. El-Rufai, in a viral video, said this is done for the faith,” Amaechi said.

He argued that appealing to religious identity for political support could deepen divisions in the country, adding that he would not encourage such an approach even if it offered him an electoral advantage.

“I wouldn’t want to run that kind of federation. There are 35 million Catholics in Nigeria. I wouldn’t want to go to the Catholic Church and say, ‘please announce me. Tell them that all Catholics must go out and vote Amaechi.’

“It will cause confusion. It will cause problems in the country. That makes me a nationalist,” he said.

Amaechi questioned the perception of Tinubu as an exceptionally strategic politician, asking why he had not become president earlier if his political success was based on an extraordinary ability to manoeuvre.

Tinubu defeated Amaechi and other aspirants at the APC presidential primary held at Eagle Square, Abuja, in June 2022, polling 1,271 votes against Amaechi’s 316.

Kemi Badenoch Tackles Trump, Says US President Deserves US Midterm Defeat

 Sunday Ehigiator

British Conservative Party leader, Kemi Badenoch, has said the United States President Donald Trump deserved his defeat in the country’s midterm elections, criticising his handling of the Iran war, trade policies and treatment of allies.

 The Independent reported yesterday that Badenoch described Trump’s electoral setback as “entirely self-inflicted” and condemned what she called his “dirty” style of politics.

The Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts in a major setback for Trump’s Republican Party.

Asked whether Trump deserved the defeat, Badenoch, in an interview with The Independent’s Editor-in-Chief, Geordie Greig, replied, “Yeah. He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative.”

She criticised Trump’s tariffs, threats towards Canada and Greenland, and disputes with US allies, saying his actions contradicted conservative principles of free markets and better trade.

 “Where is the push for free markets and better trade… rather than protectionism, America first, the squabbling with allies? That’s not what conservatives do,” she said.

Badenoch also criticised Trump’s personal attacks on journalists and political figures, saying his conduct fell below the standards expected of a statesman.

“Trump is very charming in person, but you see the way that he talks about journalists, about individuals. It doesn’t meet the standards a statesman should meet – always wanting to get dirty in terms of insults and so on,” she said.

She said she was particularly unhappy with Trump’s remarks about British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and described his treatment of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the White House as “awful”.

On the Iran war, Badenoch said she understood Trump’s initial decision to launch the military action, which she supported because of concerns about Iran acquiring nuclear weapons, but questioned the absence of a clear strategy.

“We don’t want them getting nuclear weapons. But where’s the plan?” she asked.

She also said she would have been content if Trump had lost the 2024 presidential election to his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris.

Asked which of the two candidates she preferred, Badenoch said, “I would say I like them both equally. Make of that what you will.”

The Conservative leader also argued that Trump had squandered the broad coalition of voters that helped him win the presidency, including Latino voters and more Black voters than any previous Republican candidate.

“What’s the first thing he does? Tariffs, and then talking about Greenland and Canada. A lot of people were wondering, ‘What are you doing?’” she said.

Badenoch’s comments came amid wider criticism of Trump’s handling of the economy and foreign policy following the Republicans’ losses in the midterms.

Badenoch is the leader of the UK Conservative Party and Leader of the Opposition. She became Conservative leader in November 2024 after defeating Robert Jenrick in the party’s leadership contest. She previously served as the UK’s Business and Trade Secretary and Minister for Women and Equalities under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak.

Badenoch, whose birth name is Olukemi Olufunto Adegoke, was born in Wimbledon, London, in 1980 to Nigerian parents.

news.text:
President Donald Trump faced a wave of ridicule after a sit-down interviewer asked whether he could kick one of his favorite habits.

In an interview airing Sunday on "60 Minutes," correspondent Ross Douthat asked Trump whether he could go six months without insulting Democrats if that's what it took to get a deal done. Trump insisted he could do it "very easily."

The question came after Trump brought up Senator-elect James Talarico and said Talarico had signaled on Fox News that he wanted to work with him on immigration. Douthat pointed out that Trump had occasionally mocked Talarico with the nickname "TalaFREAKo" during the campaign.

"Yeah, I did," Trump replied.

Asked whether he could work with Democrats without constantly insulting them, Trump said, "Yeah, I could," before adding that he also calls many of them "dumbocrats." Douthat noted Trump had done so only days earlier.

The network's preview clip set off a pile-on from commentators across the political spectrum.

Ron Filipkowski, a former federal prosecutor who now serves as editor-in-chief of the MeidasTouch Network, said he rarely laughs at Trump clips but couldn't believe what he was seeing on "60 Minutes."

"Trump has never sounded more weak and pathetic," he added.

David Corn, Washington bureau chief for Mother Jones, wasn't buying Trump's answer.

"I'll take that bet," Corn posted.

Matt Lewis, a conservative columnist and author of "Too Dumb to Fail," put Trump's odds far lower.

"Six months? He can't go six minutes," Lewis wrote.

British broadcaster Piers Morgan, who has interviewed Trump several times, landed in the same spot, predicting Trump would last about "six minutes before the President lapsed."

John Sailer, a conservative writer, imagined a patient waking from a 12-year coma only to find the same exchange playing on a hospital TV, capped by Trump declaring that he also calls many Democrats "dumbocrats."

Justin Hart, a conservative commentator and founder of Rational Ground, likened the interview to parenting.

"This is the same conversation I have with my 5-year-old every day about getting along with her sisters," Hart quipped.
