news.title: How China's clean-tech machine is transforming the global climate fight
news.text: China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country. In fact, the nation's green-manufacturing juggernaut, built in part through heavy ​subsidies from Beijing, nearly matches the current total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change, according to a Reuters analysis. Those loans and grants stemmed from a climate-finance program the world's wealthiest nations agreed to at a 2009 United Nations climate conference on the premise that industrialized nations made outsized contributions to the climate crisis - and had outsized means to help poorer countries pay to clean it up. A Reuters investigation in 2024 found that most global climate finance comes in the form of loans - and sometimes at market interest rates that funnel billions of dollars back to rich countries. China took a different approach, funneling billions in subsidies into its own green-energy industries, serving its own national interest to dominate next-generation manufacturing domestically and globally. The result: massive and rapid market-share gains in solar panels, batteries and battery minerals, electric vehicles, wind turbines and other green products. China remains by far the world's biggest greenhouse-gas emitter because of its large population, concentration of heavy industry and reliance on coal power. But its huge clean tech exports mean it ‌has also become among the biggest global forces in reducing climate-damaging emissions. The Reuters analysis used customs data to calculate the value of Chinese exports of clean ​technologies to countries classified by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development as developing nations. Those exports alone will help the ​Global South avoid 257 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions (MtCO2) per year once deployed - an amount equal to the annual carbon dioxide emissions of France, according to analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. This year's exports from China, meanwhile, are on track ​to avoid 337 MtCO2 in the Global South, the analysis shows. Reuters was unable to find a reliable single estimate of how much greenhouse gas emissions are avoided as a result of global climate finance from rich to poor countries. The OECD estimates a fifth of all rich world climate giving in 2024 came from the private sector. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the High Ambition Coalition - an informal coalition of nations that has advocated for substantial climate finance - did not immediately comment for this story. The $132 billion figure derived by Reuters for China's global climate contribution also includes an estimated $40 billion of Chinese foreign direct investment into clean-technology projects in developing countries. The investment data was compiled by Mathias Larsen and Xiaokang Xue at the London School of Economics. That brings China's contribution to nearly equal to the $137 billion in climate finance that wealthy nations provided to poorer ones in 2024 under their UN climate pledges, according to the most recent figures provided by the OECD. The ​figures are not directly comparable. China's total largely reflects commercial transactions focused on clean energy development, while climate finance can also support other types of programs like developing climate-resilient agricultural techniques or cleaning up damage from major storms or floods. But the comparison illustrates the extraordinary scale at which China's manufacturing economy is now shaping the energy transition in poorer countries. The findings ‌point to a potential shift in the mechanics of the global energy transition, according to Li Shuo, a veteran observer of China at UN climate talks who heads the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. For years, climate talks focused on how much ​money and technology wealthy countries would provide to poorer ones to help them decarbonize. China's manufacturing boom is creating another pathway: Driving down the price of clean technology through self-interested innovation and scale - until developing countries adopt it for economic reasons. "You can align it to your economic agenda," he said. EXPORT GIANT, DIPLOMATIC MOUSE Beijing has so far shown little interest in translating its commercial might into diplomatic leadership at global climate talks since President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from international climate cooperation in 2025. China's diplomatic role likely will take center stage as nations gather this month for the UN's COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. Bilateral agreements between heavyweights Washington and Beijing have traditionally paved the way for international climate agreements, including the ‌landmark 2015 Paris deal to limit global warming. But Beijing may be unwilling to go on alone without its geopolitical counterweight at ​the table, according to former climate negotiators. Beijing may also be worried that taking a bold stance on global carbon reduction would bring unwanted pressure ‌for China to give more climate aid or cut its own fossil-fuel emissions, observers say. China emits about a third of all carbon dioxide emissions and still burns coal for more than half its power. "How China engages on different levels in the coming years is the most fundamental thing that ‌is going to happen on climate because of both their role in clean-tech deployment… but also because of their emissions profile," said Jennifer Morgan, Germany's former climate minister. China's Ministry of Commerce said the country is an important contributor to the global green transformation, and that its wind and solar exports have cumulatively reduced global emissions ​by roughly 4.1 billion tons of CO2 over the past five years - the equivalent of around 80% of the total emissions of the United States in one year. "Against the backdrop of a global climate governance 'action deficit,' China will continue to uphold a responsible attitude, working with other countries to address challenges, overcome difficulties, and jointly promote global green and low-carbon transformation and sustainable development," it said. FORCING OUT FOSSIL FUELS Meanwhile, China's manufacturing boom has made renewable energy more affordable in the developing ​world. When Ethiopia banned combustion engine car imports in 2024, for example, it was the first country to take such a dramatic step toward electric vehicles. The decision was less about emissions and more about cutting its fuel import bill, its deputy minister of transport at the time told Reuters. "No one in Ethiopia is asking COP to pay for any of this; the economics have just switched. It is just the cheapest and best solution," said Larsen, a senior policy fellow at the London School of Economics, who built the database of Chinese green ‌investment used by Reuters in this story. China has been by far the world's biggest supplier of electric vehicles over the past few years, as dozens of subsidized automakers have waged a fierce price war in China and dramatically increased exports. The green transition has been similarly pragmatic in Pakistan, which imported 17GW worth of ‌solar from China last year, according to data from Ember, roughly on par with Germany's installations that year. Those panels will cut emissions and, more importantly, provide cheap, reliable power in a country that often has neither. Nearly two thirds of China's exports of solar panels, and the cells needed to make them, went to the developing world last year, according to Reuters analysis of customs data. The picture is different in wealthy countries like the United States and parts of Europe, which in recent years have imposed tariffs and other restrictions on Chinese clean technology to protect their domestic manufacturers from the surge in shipments. The United States, for example, imposes tariffs exceeding 100% on Chinese electric vehicles and has taken other measures to effectively block them from the market. "What is striking is that policies originally designed to address climate change are now facing opposition not because of their climate impacts, but because of concerns about trade and competitiveness," said André Corrêa do Lago, a veteran climate negotiator for Brazil, which hosted last year's climate ​summit.

news.title: Trump's Recent Warning Is Sending Shockwaves Through Wall Street. Here's What It Could Mean for Your Retirement Savings.
news.text:
Love him or hate him, President Donald Trump's time in the White House has historically correlated with strong stock market returns. In fact, the benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) is up by over 39% since his inauguration in late 2024, showcasing widespread optimism among many on Wall Street. 

So far, excitement about his pro-business policies has helped investors overlook severe macroeconomic challenges like tariffs, inflation, and unsustainable deficit spending. Let's dig deeper to see how much longer the honeymoon period might last and determine what effect the recent midterm results may have on market performance in the near term.

Why markets historically like Trump 

Like many Republican presidents, Trump has embraced a largely pro-business stance, passing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which featured tax cuts and deregulation. The administration has also struck a favorable tone toward new energy projects and data center construction, which is especially important for the U.S. tech sector as it embarks on one of its largest infrastructure buildouts in history to support generative AI. 

That said, it is increasingly clear that this one industry is helping prop up an otherwise lackluster stock market and (arguably) struggling economy.

According to CME Group, the information technology sector now accounts for a whopping 40% of the S&P 500's market cap. This level of concentration is risky in and of itself. But it is also allowing Wall Street to ignore the growing scale of macroeconomic challenges in the US. 

Trump gives a devastating warning to savers

Many of the biggest economic challenges stem from the administration's deliberate policies. These include Trump's tariffs, which have helped bring the average U.S. levy on all imports to around 9.6%, and the war in Iran, which has sent Brent crude prices up 55% since the start of the year. 

US inflation now stands at 3.7%, well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target, forcing the central bank to keep rates elevated to control consumer prices. This has also corresponded with soaring Treasury bond yields as investors get nervous about the government's ability to manage its $40 trillion in debt. 

Treasury bonds represent the risk-free rate in the economy. And when they rise, they can reduce investor appetite for risky growth stocks while also increasing the cost of capital these businesses need to expand. The Trump administration doesn't have a convincing strategy to fix these issues.

In an October interview with Time Magazine, Trump suggested that higher levels of inflation could help pay down the debt "very rapidly". The logic is that by devaluing U.S. currency, inflation will also devalue the national debt and make it easier to manage. These remarks should be taken as a warning that the administration may be willing to maintain its current inflationary fiscal policies over the coming years. 

What should investors do next?

Inflation is one of the most devastating things for investors and retirement savers because it constantly erodes both savings and financial market returns. Even if you earn the S&P 500's average annual return of 10%, an inflation rate of 3.7% takes your real rate of return to a much less impressive 6.3%. That said, this isn't the time to panic. 

Over the long haul, the U.S. has shown a remarkable ability to self-correct and bounce back from crises, and this time probably won't be the exception. The recent midterm results could impose some checks and balances on the Iran war and on some of the government's most extreme spending plans (such as a proposed $1.5 trillion military budget), which could help calm the bond market and bring down inflation. 

Yes, the U.S. economic situation remains uncertain, but there may be light at the end of the tunnel. Investors should also focus on diversifying their portfolios across a variety of asset classes to avoid being overly exposed to downside risk in any particular one.

news.title: Midterm surprise
news.text:
THAT the Republican Party would lose the midterm elections for the US Congress was never in doubt. It was its overwhelming defeat that surprised everyone. Demo-crats have attained a clear majority in the 100-member US Senate (54 Demo-crats, 44 Republicans) and a massive lead in the 435-member House of Represen-tatives (253 Democrats, 157 Republicans). What explains this major shift? One plausible answer is the Iran war and its effects on gas prices, inflation, and the higher cost of living. Importantly, America’s younger population never owned this war. It has been widely seen as Israel’s war that America was fighting. Vice President J.D. Vance has rightly concluded that “the reason we lost [in the elections] is the war”. Even Donald Trump acknowledged that the war with Iran was a factor, though he defended its objectives.

While the Iran war and its side effects may have been the main reason for the Republicans’ defeat, several other factors also weighed in. In his election campaigns, Trump had opposed distant wars, yet he entered into one with Iran at the behest of Israel. American voters saw this as a clear repudiation of the ‘America First’ approach that Trump had touted in his speeches. It was hard for Americans to accept America’s subordination to Israeli interests. This, in turn, raised questions about US legislators’ links with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, whose activities are aligned closely with the agenda of a foreign government (Israel), Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and US complicity by continuing to provide weapons and assistance to Israel. All this did not sit well with young Americans.

How will it impact America’s foreign policy? Two aspects merit attention. First, Trump is unlikely to resume the war with Iran or follow through on his threats to use the mother of all bombs against Iran. The reason is clear. His Republican Party will not want a return to a war that is so unpopular with Americans. A return to war could jeopardise the party’s future stakes, including the race for the White House. In fact, America would like to see an honourable exit from the war. The answer lies in diplomacy and a return to the Islamabad MoU, which meets both the key US demand that Iran should not produce nuclear weapons and the Iranian demand that economic sanctions be lifted and Iran’s frozen assets released. This provides an honourable off-ramp to both sides to end a war that serves no one but Israel.

As for the Strait of Hormuz, everyone wants it to reopen fully because disrupted supplies of oil, gas, petroleum products, and fertilisers have been hurting the world economy. To that end, America should end its naval blockade, and Iran should agree not to interrupt shipping in the strait. All these points have been amply covered in the Islamabad MoU. The parties to the Makkah Agreement — Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye — have a special role. They must increase their diplomatic efforts, as should Qatar and Oman. Even China and Russia may need to step in to help find a diplomatic solution. China, in particular, has an interest in ensuring fuel supplies and the smooth functioning of markets. The window of opportunity may be limited, as the caretaker Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, might plan some manoeuvre, a false flag operation, or some drastic action like using a tactical nuclear weapon to force Iran to respond and then rope the US into the war with Iran.

 Republicans will not want to return to a war unpopular with Americans.

The second aspect of US foreign policy relevant to us is whether it will affect Pakistan-US ties. The latter have always been transactional and viewed through America’s own geopolitical interests. As of now, post-Ma-rka-i-Haq Pakistan continues to enjoy respect as a stabilising force in the region. Further, gi--ven that Afgha-nis-tan is once again becoming a safe haven for the wor-ld’s terrorist organisations, Pakistan’s geopolitical importance as the only state fighting terrorism in all its forms, including proxy terrorism by India from Afghanistan, will remain valid. Pakistan has flourishing bilateral trade with the US, along with cooperation in multiple areas, including agriculture and IT. Relations between Pakistan and the US are, thus, likely to continue at their own pace.

Although many in the ranks of the De--mocrats tend to have pro-Israel, pro-India, anti-Iran, and anti-China sentiments — si--m---ilar to the Republicans — American foreign policy will remain a major subject of discussion in the Democrats-dominated Con---gress in the months ahead. Trans-at-la-n-tic allian-ces, relations with Canada, adventures like Venezuela, opposition to climate change, tariff wars, Islamophobia, subservience to Israeli interests, and Trump’s refusal to regulate AI technologies could all be up for review when the re-composed Congress starts its work next January.

The writer is a former foreign secretary of Pakistan.

news.title: From deep in Trump country, farmers sent a message to Washington
news.text:
Fred Levendofsky has worked the land in rural Kansas for over half a century and, like many farmers here, was a fervent backer of Donald Trump.

Across the US Midwest, agricultural communities have been among the president's most fierce defenders and reliable supporters.

Mr Levendofsky, 68, voted for Trump twice. But not a third time.

Two years into Mr Trump's second term, Mr Levendofsky's overheads have skyrocketed.

The cost of diesel fuel he uses to run machinery and vehicles has increased by about 40 per cent from last year, and his total expenses have jumped by about 50 per cent.

"How long are we going to wear the cost? Things need to change," he told the ABC from his 360-hectare farm in the state's north.

This week they did. Kansas has sent senators from Mr Trump's Republican Party to Washington DC for almost a century but at Tuesday's midterm elections, Democrat Adam Hamilton claimed a comfortable win.

The GOP incumbent, a physician worth an estimated several million dollars, faced criticism after the New York Times reported that his former obstetrics practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills and charged an 18 per cent annual interest rate. Mr Marshall called the report a "hit job".

Riding a wave of anti-Trump sentiment around the country, the Democrats surged in both the House and Senate races to take control of both chambers. It means the president's political life over the final two years of his term will be more difficult, although he still wields immense power.

While Kansas had been safe Republican ground for generations, the GOP top brass had grown increasingly worried that Marshall would lose, and pulled out all the stops to save the seat.

The party was so concerned that the president made a last-minute stop in the state last weekend to hold a rally in a bid to energise his base.

It did not work. Marshall still lost convincingly to megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, who pitched himself as a religious centrist who would bring decency back to American politics.

"I'm glad a message was sent to Washington," Fred Levendofsky told the ABC.

"I'd hope that now we've got a Democrat-controlled House and Senate, that they'll work with Mr Trump and hopefully they can sort this oil issue."

While soaring fuel costs are something being felt around America — and it is particularly pronounced in Kansas — people's gripes with the federal government run much deeper.

The war in Iran, and the billions of dollars being spent on it, is deeply unpopular. The president's multiple trade wars have also hurt the farmers' bottom lines.

"Things just aren't working; it's all going backwards," said Nick Levendofsky, Fred's 41-year-old son and a senior member of the state's farmers' union.

International demand for Kansas cereal, grain and beef has withered due to China's retaliation to the Trump administration's sweeping tariffs.

The White House announced an assistance package for farmers late last year, in which they could claim one-off lump sums of cash linked to the size of your land.

"It doesn't matter how big a farm you are, you're dealing with these same issues and I think more than anything, they want a market. We want trade, not aid," Nick said.

"Frankly, the government cheques aren't even covering our losses and, you know, farmers have lost over $US40 billion ($58.3 billion) since the trade war started. It's probably way more than that now."

Both the Levendofskys were once registered Republicans but are hoping their state's new blue senator can help stand up to the president.

"As far as what he did when we did the war with Iran, I do think they needed to stop the business with nuclear weapons, I understand that and I understand we all as Americans probably need to shoulder some of that expense," Fred told the ABC.

"It's been very difficult. A year ago, we were able to harvest the grain, and at the end of the year I was able to sell the grain and pay my expenses on the crops and had a little bit left over.

"This year, that's not going to happen. We probably won't even have enough to pay for the fertiliser and seed because of the increase in fuel."

While Kansas commands just six Electoral College votes in presidential contests, the erosion of Donald Trump's rural base — collapsing by more than 30 percentage points in some precincts — suggests the party can be competitive in territories once deemed hostile.

The Democrats flipped Republican Senate seats in Texas, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Iowa this week, and remain a chance to take two more in Mississippi and Alaska, too. Many of those states had backed the Republicans for decades.

"We're looking at a political opportunity for the Democrats not seen since Watergate," said Matt Harris, a political scientist at Park University in neighbouring Missouri, told the ABC.

"Kansas now has to be on the table in the presidential elections.

"And I think this shift speaks to the dissatisfaction about the economy, the dissatisfaction about some of the choices that the Trump administration has made, but I think for Democrats, the message is: what are you going to do to deliver on those things?"

During his victory speech on Tuesday evening, Mr Hamilton wore a pin that said "love one another" and stressed the need for people on both sides of politics to work together.

Buoyed by the party's historic victory this week, Democrats are hoping they can continue to build momentum in the state when the next presidential election is held in two years' time.

"Kansas doesn't have a lot of Democrats, but people wanted change," Nick Levendofsky said.

"We want moderate politics back in Kansas, and I think the senator-elect is hopefully going to deliver on that."
news.summary: Fred Levendofsky and his son Nick have worked the land in rural Kansas for over half a century and were fervent backers of Donald Trump, but not any more.

 International News, Latest News 

November 7, 2026




 Israel president taps Eisenkot to form new government 







Jerusalem, (AFP) — Israel’s president announced on Saturday he would task Gadi Eisenkot with forming the next government following last week’s election, in what Netanyahu’s rivals see as a first step to remove the country’s longest-serving prime minister.

The opposition bloc led by Eisenkot, a former military chief and political newcomer who has tried to appeal to secular and liberal Israelis, has opened the door to a once improbable alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jews, which could give it the numbers to form a coalition.

President Isaac Herzog said that after consultations with all parties during the week, he would grant Eisenkot the first chance to form a government after the October 27 election, in which neither side secured a majority in a country deeply polarised by Netanyahu’s hard-right rule and worn down by three years of war.

The formal appointment would take place in an official ceremony on Sunday at the president’s residence in Jerusalem, Herzog’s office said.

Eisenkot was recommended by parties representing 67 lawmakers as opposed to 46 for Netanyahu’s bloc.

But the recommendations for Eisenkot included members of Israel’s Arab minority — whose seat haul soared in the election on the back of anger against Netanyahu — and right-leaning segments of the opposition oppose relying on Arab votes.

– Netanyahu pushes unity government –

Herzog, who originally came from Israel’s now defunct left-wing Labour Party but who has a non-partisan role and has forged a working relationship with Netanyahu, has signalled that he would like to explore a national unity government that would seek to bring together Jewish Israelis from across the political spectrum.

Pressure for a unity government could build if Netanyahu follows through on threats to resume war on Iran, although US President Donald Trump has not given the green light and received his own drubbing in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Netanyahu, who has led Israel on and off for nearly two decades and guided its sharply rightward turn in recent years, faces corruption charges and potentially jail if he leaves office. He also faces an arrest warrant over the Gaza war from the International Criminal Court, whose authority he rejects.

Netanyahu has already called for a unity government but the opposition has stood firm on removing him first.

He has attacked opposition leaders for even considering working with Israeli Arabs, descendants of Palestinians who stayed after the creation of Israel in 1948.

The incumbent premier said on Saturday that a potential coalition between opposition parties and Arab lists, which he called Islamists, would “dismantle the State of Israel from within” and urged the formation of a unity government comprising “all the Zionist parties that want to safeguard our state.”

In response, Eisenkot’s Yashar party urged Netanyahu’s allies and members of his Likud party to form a unity government led by Eisenkot and to “publicly announce the dissolution of their alliance with the extremists”.

Opposition bloc member Avigdor Liberman, a former Netanyahu aide turned fierce critic who nonetheless shares his hawkish views on the Palestinians, has made clear that he will not sit with Eisenkot if he relies on Israeli-Arab votes.

But on Friday, Liberman — a staunch secularist whose support base initially was Russian-speaking immigrants — made a U-turn on another group he had shunned and said he was open to discussions on a law that would enshrine an exemption for ultra-Orthodox Jews from mandatory military service.

Liberman and another opposition leader, Naftali Bennett, had made closing the exemption a core campaign promise and had viscerally criticised ultra-Orthodox Jews as burdens on the state, responding to wide resentment by other Israelis at a time when reservists are serving multiple tours in Gaza and Lebanon.

Eisenkot has proposed requiring national service for all Israelis but allowing citizens to choose a civilian option rather than the military, opening the door to integrating the ultra-Orthodox.

In a message delivered on Friday before Israel shut down for the sabbath, Eisenkot said it was urgent to replace Netanyahu, calling him a threat to the “very existence of Israeli democracy”.

He called for the swift formation of a government, which could initially rely on outside support, with more parties joining eventually.

Following his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.

If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 due to repeated deadlocks.

news.title: Lessons from US Midterm Elections for Nigeria in 2027
news.text:
The resounding defeat of Republicans by Democrats in the United States’ midterm elections does not only serve as a reminder to the ruling All Progressives Congress that electoral victories are not permanent endorsements of political parties and their leaders but a lesson to the Independent National Electoral Commission on how it should ensure that public confidence in an election is not in doubt, Wale Igbintade writes

Tsunami, a stunning rebuke, judgement, trouncing, complete repudiation, referendum, crushing, and landslide were some of the various words used to describe the Democrats’ defeat of the Republicans in the United States’ midterm elections held last Tuesday.

The outcome of the polls sent a clear message to President Donald Trump that his remaining two years in office would not be without political resistance.

For a long time to come, the midterm elections would be remembered by many Americans, particularly those who had hoped for a change in the balance of power in Congress.

In what many described as an end to the reign of terror, the Democratic Party broke several decades-long Republican winning streaks, recorded historic firsts and flipped both chambers of Congress. Voters in states and districts that had supported Trump’s re-election just two years earlier delivered a harsh verdict on his administration’s policies, including steep tariffs, rising fuel prices, corruption allegations, hardline immigration enforcement policies and the unresolved conflict with Iran.

By the time the results were announced, Democrats had secured 255 seats in the House of Representatives and 54 in the Senate, while Republicans won 134 seats in the House and 44 in the Senate. The results marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Washington.

The Democratic gains extended into territories Trump had carried comfortably in 2024, including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. 

Democrat James Talarico, who won the Senate election in Texas, attributed his victory to a different approach to politics.

“We didn’t win this race by alienating our neighbours or shaming our neighbours or ridiculing our neighbours. We embodied a new kind of politics. A politics rooted in a deep love for our state, for our country and, most importantly, for all of our neighbours,” he said.

Before the elections, Trump had urged supporters to vote as though he were on the ballot. After the results, however, he claimed on social media that he would have won “IN A LANDSLIDE!” 

The results suggested otherwise, with voters appearing to judge his administration’s performance.

Reportedly, 62 per cent of voters disapproved of his performance, while 38 per cent approved. Nearly 90 per cent identified the cost of living as a major factor in their vote, while nearly two-thirds believed his policies had worsened the economy. More than half also expressed reservations about his leadership and priorities.

Trump’s interventions in the closing days of the campaign also appeared to backfire, with controversial remarks attracting attention away from his party’s agenda.

The question now is how Trump will respond to the setback. Known for his combative approach to criticism, he has said he would accept the election results and work with Democrats. Whether he will maintain that position remains to be seen.

Democratic control of Congress gives the party greater leverage to challenge Trump’s agenda, including his tariffs, healthcare policies and military actions in Iran. The House could also investigate allegations of profiteering involving his family and associates, while impeachment proceedings have been raised as a possibility.

Inside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results quickly gave way to anger with Trump. They argued that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party the elections. Some said the president dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington.

Unlike what he did in the presidential election in 2024 when Trump was on the ballot, not even the about $500million the billionaire businessman Elon Musk, put down to boost Republicans chances in the polls save the day.

As Nigeria approaches its 2027 general election, the American experience raises questions about whether voters will similarly use the ballot to express dissatisfaction with an incumbent government. Many Nigerians are grappling with economic hardship, inflation, insecurity, corruption, inadequate electricity and poor infrastructure, among other challenges.

The American experience raises questions about whether voters in Nigeria will similarly use the ballot to express dissatisfaction with President Bola Tinubu and other candidates of his All Progressives Congress (APC) as the country approaches its 2027 elections. This is because economic grievances that contributed to the Republican defeat are not alien to Nigeria where Nigerians face many of them in far more debilitating circumstances.

Economic hardship necessitated by cost of food, transportation, healthcare, electricity, corruption, nepotism, deplorable roads and insecurity has placed unbearable pressure on households. Inflation has diminished purchasing power, while government policies have imposed enormous adjustment costs on ordinary citizens. Millions are struggling to cope with economic hardship, even as those in positions of authority offer explanations, justifications and assurances.

Beyond the economy, questions of democratic accountability, institutional independence, governance and the exercise of executive power remain central to Nigeria’s political discourse. These are fundamental to the survival of any functioning democracy.

Despite the hardship and insecurity in the country, APC is confident that it would win the election in landslide.

Those who spoke to THISDAY urged Nigerians to use similar factors to rate and assess the ruling APC in 2027, citing the defeat of the Republicans as an example of how citizens can hold governments accountable through the ballot box.

Their views point to a central question ahead of the election: will Nigerians primarily judge the APC-led federal government by its record in office or will political loyalty, regional identity, ethnicity, religious bigotry, financial inducements and party machinery play a more decisive role?

A lawyer, Samson Afegbai, identified five issues that could influence the election: Insecurity, foreign exchange, the government’s subsidy policy, the cost of living and infrastructure. Femi Adeyinka similarly identified the economy as a decisive factor.

He feels that the removal of the petrol subsidy and the unification of the foreign exchange market under Tinubu have had significant implications for fuel prices, transportation and purchasing power. Although the government has defended the reforms as necessary to correct longstanding economic distortions, voters will be interested in whether they translate into tangible improvements in living conditions before 2027.

The candidates must therefore demonstrate how their economic policies can improve household incomes, employment, electricity supply and business conditions. While Tinubu will be judged on his administration’s record, Atiku and Obi must convince voters that their alternatives offer a credible route to recovery.

Another respondent and businessman, Emeka Odittah, identified six factors that could shape the election: The economy, coalition-building, voter turnout, security, religion and zoning, and the credibility of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

The businessman placed particular emphasis on electoral credibility, arguing that public confidence in the voting and result-transmission processes could influence participation and acceptance of the outcome. He said the credibility of INEC, particularly the use of the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, the INEC Result Viewing Portal and the collation of results, would be crucial to public confidence in the election.

According to Odittah, the 2027 contest would be shaped by economic hardship and the ability of candidates to build cross-regional coalitions while securing public trust in the electoral process.

This is why the ADC urged Nigerians to draw lessons from the American elections and vote out the APC in 2027.

In a statement issued by its National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi, the party drew parallels between the American elections and Nigeria’s political situation under President Tinubu, arguing that voters should prioritise their welfare over political loyalty, sentiments and the personalities of political leaders.

“Americans have shown that when politicians become arrogant, when policies punish ordinary people, and when those in power mistake popularity for a permanent licence to govern, the ballot box remains the ultimate instrument of accountability,” the party said.

The ADC urged Nigerians to consider the country’s economic and security challenges before deciding whether to renew the APC’s mandate. It accused the Tinubu administration of presiding over worsening economic hardship, insecurity and declining opportunities, arguing that the ruling party should not be rewarded with another term.

“We cannot continue to complain about the cost of living while voting for a President who has made life unaffordable. We cannot demand security while rewarding failure,” the party said.

For the Human Rights Writers Association of Nigeria (HURIWA), the outcome of the US midterm elections should serve as an important lesson to Nigeria’s electoral authorities and political leaders on the need to guarantee credible, transparent and peaceful elections.

In a statement by its National Coordinator, Emmanuel Onwubiko, the group stressed that the victories by Democratic candidates and the transfer of control of both chambers of the Congress demonstrated the importance of allowing voters to determine political outcomes through credible electoral processes.

HURIWA argued that electoral credibility is strengthened when voters can independently verify results and political parties have confidence that the declared outcome reflects the ballots cast. It called on the Chairman of INEC, Professor Joash Amupitan, and other election managers to draw lessons from established democracies and ensure that Nigeria’s January 2027 national elections are free, fair, transparent and peaceful. It also warned that any attempt to manipulate the 2027 elections could trigger serious political instability and undermine public confidence in constitutional democracy.

The American experience offers a reminder that electoral victories are not permanent endorsements of political parties or their leaders. But whether Nigerians will apply that lesson in 2027 remains to be seen.

news.title: Gulf On Edge: Blasts Hit Iran's Hormuz Coast, US Disables Cargo Ship As Houthis Target Ara
news.text: Fighting flared on two fronts in the Gulf over the weekend. It began just as oil markets had started pricing in an end to the eight-month US-Iran war.Late on Saturday, explosions were reported along Iran's southern coast. Iranian state media named Qeshm Island, which sits inside the Strait of Hormuz, along with the ports of Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas. Hours later, the navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two oil tankers had hit sea mines while using what it called an unauthorised route through the strait.Separately, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had launched six missile and drone attacks on Saturday. The targets included Saudi Aramco installations, Riyadh's main airport and Saudi military positions.Mine claims and coastal blastsThe IRGC Navy said the two tankers had switched off their tracking systems. It said both ships caught fire, were badly damaged and stopped moving. It did not name the ships or say where they were headed. There has been no independent confirmation of Iran's account.Iranian authorities have not formally explained the coastal blasts. Tasnim, a semi-official news agency, first reported that two missiles had hit Qeshm. It later carried a source who denied any missile strike. Iranian state television linked the sounds to military activity in the strait. Iran has made similar mine claims almost every day in recent weeks.US fires on blockade runnerUS Central Command (CENTCOM) said a US military aircraft fired precision-guided munitions at the stern of the M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday. The ship is St. Kitts and Nevis-flagged. CENTCOM said the civilian crew had ignored repeated warnings and tried several times to get past Washington's naval blockade of Iran.CENTCOM said its forces first told the crew to “abandon the targeted spaces” on board. According to the command, the ship had called at an Iranian port and was trying to leave regional waters.The Huda is a 24,993-deadweight-tonne dry bulk carrier built in 1999 and managed from Turkey, according to The Maritime Executive. The publication said the ship did not appear to be under sanctions. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) placed the ship about 18 nautical miles east of Khor Fakkan in the UAE and said it did not know the crew's condition.This is the first ship the US has reported disabling since October 10. On that date it struck the bulk carrier Ocean Molica, also in the Gulf of Oman. CENTCOM said 147 commercial vessels have been redirected since the blockade restarted in mid-July. In the same period, five vessels that refused to comply have been disabled.The weekend's events follow US strikes on Qeshm earlier in the week. US officials described those strikes as limited and defensive. In a Fox News interview, President Donald Trump said Iran had spent about two months building an anti-aircraft site on the island. “As soon as it was completed — we hit it,” Trump said.UKMTO data show the pressure on shipping is not easing. It recorded six confirmed attacks in the region in the first days of November and five more in late October. By its count, 133 vessels have been damaged in the region so far this year.Houthis widen attacks on Saudi oil assetsAcross the Arabian Peninsula, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree listed the group's targets for Saturday. He said it hit King Khalid International Airport and Aramco oil storage tanks and a distillation tower in Riyadh. He also named an Aramco facility at Khurais in the Eastern Province and Pumping Station No. 8 at Dawadmi, west of the capital.Saree said the group used “a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles” and drones. He said the other three attacks targeted a Saudi National Guard camp in Najran and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen's Al-Jawf and Marib provinces. He gave no casualty figures that could be checked.Saudi Arabia did not immediately confirm any damage. The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a Houthi cruise missile fired towards Riyadh on Saturday. Saudi Civil Defence briefly issued a threat alert for Najran and lifted it about 10 minutes later.The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for air strikes they blame on Saudi Arabia. Those include strikes on Saturday on homes in the Bani Hushaysh district east of Sanaa. Houthi-run media and health officials put the death toll there at between 25 and more than 30, many of them women and children. The Houthis also cite a deadly strike on a market in Taiz province a day earlier. The coalition did not comment on the casualty reports.ALSO READ: 'Can Do That In 10 Mins': Trump Renews Threat To Strike Iran's Pickaxe MountainFighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has picked up sharply since July, when a truce largely broke down. Since then, airports and oil facilities have been among the group's main targets inside the kingdom.What it means for oilThe weekend escalation follows a week in which crude prices fell steeply. Brent settled 3 cents higher at $98.32 a barrel on Friday and fell more than 16% over the week. Traders had bet on a diplomatic breakthrough after the US midterm elections. WTI settled at $90.83.Not everyone in the market believes the conflict is over. Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy Group, told CNBC he sees an 80% chance that fighting resumes. He said both benchmarks could go back above $100 a barrel.Markets reopen on Monday. Traders will be watching whether the mine claims near Hormuz and the Houthi strikes on Aramco's Eastern Province and pipeline sites bring back some of the risk premium that came out of oil prices last week.ALSO READ: US Offers $20 Million Reward For Information On Iran's Nuclear Programme

news.title: Western nations provide Ukraine with $212 bln worth financial aid since February 2022
news.text:
MOSCOW, November 8. /TASS/. Western nations and international institutions have provided Ukraine with nearly $212 bln in direct financial support through various grants and loans since February 2022, according to TASS calculations based on data from the Ukrainian Ministry of Finance.

The amount given was allocated directly to the Ukrainian state budget and does not include military aid provided through the transfer of weapons, hardware, ammunition, equipment, and intelligence, as well as the training of Ukrainian army units.

The European Union was Kiev's largest donor, providing Ukraine with over $85 bln. The United States provided financial aid to Ukraine under the Joe Biden administration (2021-2025), but Donald Trump halted it upon entering the White House in January 2025. Nevertheless, during the Biden administration's tenure, Washington managed to transfer $30.2 bln to Kiev. Since February 2022, Ukraine has received approximately $15.6 bln from the IMF, $10.3 bln from Japan, $6.2 bln from Canada, $6.1 bln from the World Bank, and $3.8 bln from the United Kingdom. Kiev also received bilateral financial assistance and loans from individual EU member states, including around $1.7 bln from Germany, $717 million from Norway, and $437 million from France.

The Russian side has repeatedly stated that Western aid to Ukraine will not become a magic pill capable of influencing the course of the hostilities.

news.title: King Charles would 'carefully' consider China visit
news.text: LONDON, United Kingdom — A British monarch has only ever made one state visit to China: Queen Elizabeth II four decades ago. King Charles III would consider undertaking the second, according to an aide.'If the government said, 'Will the king go to China?' I think, you know we think about it very carefully,' a senior palace aide told reporters this week.The late queen, Charles's mother, visited China with her husband Prince Philip in October 1986.The trip included stops in Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou, according to reports at the time.It came two years after the signing of the Sino-British Joint Declaration setting out the terms for the return of Hong Kong, which improved relations between the two countries.'This is the 40th anniversary of the last state visit,' noted the aide, speaking at the end of the king's nine-day tour of the Caribbean.Charles's trip was dominated by the thorny subject of slavery reparations. He called the transatlantic slave trade a 'monstrous injustice' as the UK government mulls an apology.'I think what we're seeing is a very clear pattern emerging of the government asking the king to head into quite politically charged situations, quite challenging situations,' said the aide.The king, who is politically neutral, 'relishes' the 'tough parts' of his role and can be a 'great secret weapon' for the government, the aide added.'Whether that's leading on the environment, whether it's renewing and refreshing and reinvigorating relationships with nations where there have been some complex political issues at play, that is what he lives and breathes for,' they said.Charles, who is nearly 78 and still being treated for an undisclosed cancer, was widely praised for his state visit to the United States and delicate handling of US President Donald Trump earlier this year.Relations between London and Beijing have been strained for years, fuelled in part by tensions over the political situation in former British colony Hong Kong, criticism of Beijing's human rights record and spying allegations.But UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is now pursuing the same policy of cautious rapprochement started by his predecessor Keir Starmer, who visited Beijing in January.'China is a hugely important country. It's a very complex country. It would pose you know a lot of complexity in putting a program together,' Charles's aide said.As then prince of Wales, Charles oversaw Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule as Britain's most senior representative at the 1997 handover alongside China's then president Jiang Zemin.Asked whether Burnham would be asking the king to visit China, his spokesman told AFP that questions about the monarch's travel was 'one for the palace'.

news.title: UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
news.text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. -- President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.

Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.

The video featured in the media player above is the ABC7 Los Angeles 24/7 streaming channel

White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.

When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, "Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already."

He declined to say what conversations he'd had with Trump but said, "I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."

Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words "On to the next chapter."

The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.

Trump said in his post that he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as "assistants," adding, "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!"

While White didn't make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States, he did elsewhere in his news conference describe his ambitions to expand the Zuffa Boxing organization he also runs with Saudi Arabian backers and hold more of its events around the world.

Trump's post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.

The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance before reporters before leaving the job after five days.

The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.

Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.

He brought White and the sport to the White House's South Lawn in June for the celebration of America's 250th year of its independence and the president's own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under " The Claw," a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.

"It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one," said White afterward.

White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

Associated Press writers Daniel Gelston in Philadelphia and Jesse Bedayn in Austin, Texas, contributed to this report.
news.summary: UFC boss Dana White said he plans to meet with President Donald Trump on Monday after being offered the job of White House press secretary.

news.title: Trump: The Perils of Bad Manners
news.text:
Engagements with Chidi Amuta

The United States Mid Term elections have come and gone. They have left an untidy rubble with an ill-mannered despotic president, a badly injured Republican party and badly damaged institutions of the American state. The ultimate outcome of a toppling of the Republican majority in Congress may be a salvaging of American democracy and the institutional framework of the nation. But if Trump remains in the White House, the threat to America’s democracy may persist as he resorts to endless vetoes to plough his way forward.

At the worst, Donald Trump could be impeached and sent packing from the White House.

At the best, his presidency could be tempered by the norms of democratic civility. The latter possibility, Trump will cease to be Trump. Less bluster. Fewer audacious lies. There may be less strategic blunders and playing with dangerous war planes, missiles and drones. Hopefully, there will now be greater respect for the rules based international order and more respect for the international community of nations and its leaders who have endured two years of Donald Trump’s unwarranted insults and habitual diplomatic bad manners. But the US constitution still leaves a sinking Trump with a desperate lifeline: the power to veto whatever Congress decides and he disagrees with.

The impending relief is systemic. Just when both Americans and the wider world had lost hope in the survival of the show place of democracy, the American electorate hit the reverse button. The just concluded Mid Term elections into governorship and congressional seats has begun the reversal of the draining of Donald Trump’s Washington swamp. A president who initially swore he was out to drain the swamp in Washington became himself a personification of the swamp. He rode rough shod on Congress, exploiting his party’s congressional majority in both houses to literally run the United States more like an authoritarian Banana Republic. He tested the American judiciary by putting nearly all his authoritarian whims to judicial test. The Supreme Court just managed to retain a precarious integrity by reserving interim rulings on virtually everything from demolitions of sections of the White House to erect a controversial Ball Room or a laughable ‘reflective pool’. Even tangential ego driven skirmishes like renaming the Kennedy Centre and every street corner after himself became subjects of unrelenting litigations and contentious judicial pronouncements.

Over and above his many domestic excesses, Donald Trump saw the rest of the world as an adolescent playing field to test his many illusions of power and illiterate readings of power, politics and international affairs. He invaded nations within reach, imposed silly tariffs on literally every nation in the world and talked down on virtually all respectable leaders. He spoke to and about the United Nations in condescending language unheard in its chambers since after its formation in 1945. And because of America’s considerable economic and military strategic prowess, most of the world looked on in consternation and awe as the great American democratic Olympus tottered and towered over all in unsightly apparel and unbecoming language.

Matters would have been easier if the effect of Donald Trump’s wrecking ball autocracy was limited to the United States and its immediate neighbourhood. Not quite. Under the illusion of being thought strong but actually afraid of his own weakness, Trump launched a hazy war against Iran. Egged on by his cabinet of adolescent secretaries especially a certain infantile Pete Hegseth, Trump has in the last eight months hurled any number of missiles, bombs and drones at Iran with questionable impact except a pro-Zionist propaganda of conquest. Iran is of course far from being humiliated or defeated in any sense. Instead, US allies in the Middle East have all been dragged into a war they never prepared for or envisaged. Unlikely places like Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha, Aman, Riyadh and other previously peaceful places have become targets of Iran reprisal drone and rocket attacks. An entire region has been plunged into war at the behest of President Trump and his partner, Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, a man wanted abroad by the ICC for myriad human rights abuse crimes and at home for many corruption charges. Even far off places like Europe bore the brunt of Trump’s tactless foreign escapades.

At home, President Trump is alleged to have exploited his office for corrupt ends. His family is known to pursue multiple business interests all around the world where the US has interests. The president has himself engaged in insider trading in companies that have business with the US government. Not to talk of multiple rackets in crypto currency and murky deals in Venezuelan oil.

Donald Trump’s authoritarian inclinations and compulsive corruption would have paled into insignificance if the US domestic economy under his presidency enabled the ordinary American to enjoy an affordable normal life. On the contrary, the endless war with Iran has turned the strategic Strait of Hormuz into a death bed for ships of all nations and made oil cargo traffic a nightmare for strong and weak nations. Global oil process have since shot through the roof. Gasoline pump prices in America have shot up from a little over $2 before the war to more than $4 in the Mid Term week. Prices in grocery shops have taken a similar hike. In general, all those who voted for Donald Trump two years ago are all writhing under the pain of economic hardship. Therefore, the outcome of the Mid Terms was very predictable. That is the reality that has unfolded before our very eyes.

All that was left to save the world from the Trumpian ultimate nightmare was a test of the democratic core of America through the Mid Terms. It was a historic test of the democratic state. The American voter was once again called upon to use the power of the ballot to tame the autocratic inclinations of the president through a revalidation of the mandate of members of Congress as representatives of the people. Here lies the import of the Mid Terms as an instrument for the revalidation of the popular will in America’s democracy.

In the delicate balance between the individual leader and the institutions of the democratic state, Trump weighed too heavily as an elected leader. He literally overwhelmed the state and disorganized it. Congress, the judiciary, law enforcement, the federal bureaucracy, were all bent and twisted to conform to the wishes of an authoritarian “king” Trump. In the post Midterm reclamation period, there will be stresses and strains between the president and the institutions he has already mangled. The major one will be the clashes between the rescued institutions of state and the stubborn idiosyncratic tendencies of an authoritarian president. Trump will remain recalcitrant, belligerent, abusive, defiant of rules and inclined to lawlessness. Under the guise of applying the rules of business deal making, Try will try to flout the rules of diplomatic negotiation and structured engagement for his personal advantage and the benefit of his family, friends, associates and cronies. The remaining Trump tenure will remain a terrain dominated by the Elon Musks of this world.

By way of a general backdrop, the thrashing of the Trump presidency in the just concluded Midterms is a consequence of the wider implications of Trump’s political misadventure and historic displacement. For over two centuries, it was a dream that attracted all from every corner of the world. The pull of America was in its diversity, the freedom of its society, its robust spirit of enterprise that made every one that lived in America a partaker in a legacy of prosperity in a free society. The American dream came to be a shared dream of everyone that was born in or moved to live in America. Simply put, the American dream boiled down to the right of everyone in America to join the race for the pursuit of happiness through hard work, focused aspiration and an entitlement to the fruits of honest labour.

But under our very eyes, in our own life time, the American dream has turned into a nightmare. The land where everyone fled to as a last resort of freedom and safety has become an unwelcome hellhole. So called illegal immigrants are being hounded and chased around major American cities and shot on the streets in broad day light like mad dogs by untrained and bigoted immigration hounds. In the name of anti-immigration, innocent settlers some of whom have lived in America for upwards of 3-4 decades have been hounded down, loaded into war planes and deported to countries that they left many years ago without memories. 

The reign of Donald Trump as a second term President has witnessed the systematic erosion of everything that distinguished America as a civilizational force. It is now a dark force, a force of ill both at home and abroad. America under Trump has become an anti Islamic force but a Zionist champion, a bigoted white supremacist bastion. Its society is divided along racial, perception lines.

The US Mid Terms may have come as a much needed check on authoritarian drifts of the system. The president now has to obtain the authority of a more diverse congress to engage in further flirtations. But the damage that Trump’s authoritarian flirtations have done to the world and the US system is considerable. He has waged wars without congressional approval. He has killed people in open seas without caring to prove that they committed any crimes. He has livid war against sovereign states without anyone’s approval but only his instincts. He has deployed aircraft carriers into the seas of the world, ordered precision bombings, allowed the deployment of advanced missiles systems and aircraft only by a phone call to his adolescent Secretary of War. 

The abiding question now is: how does the world recover from the vast damages done to America and the world in the wild days when democracy went unguarded under the rampaging assault of an unrepentant autocrat who was however elected by a democracy. An elaborate repair job stares America in the face with a menacing urgency. The guardrails of democratic civility need to be rebuilt. Washington needs to re-cultivate decent political manners and rhetoric. Above all, America needs to unlearn the kind of vulgarity in the presidency that elevates Mickey Minaj’s bum into a subject for a presidential public utterance.

news.title: Stocks rally 7,477 points in strong weekly recovery
news.text:
KARACHI: The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) staged a strong recovery in the first week of November after October’s bearish spell, with the benchmark KSE-100 index gaining 4.5 per cent as falling international oil prices, easing inflation and hopes of reduced geopolitical tensions lifted investor sentiment.

The index rose 7,477 points to close at 173,887 points on Friday from 166,409 points in the previous week, according to Arif Habib Ltd (AHL).

AKD Securities Ltd attributed the rally to a 15.9pc weekly decline in Brent crude prices to $98.8 per barrel, following diplomatic efforts to ease tensions in the Middle East and the outcome of the US midterm elections. Democrats’ surge in Congress fuelled expectations of a possible reassessment of President Donald Trump’s foreign policy and a reduction in regional tensions.

However, analysts cautioned that market direction would remain sensitive to developments in US-Iran negotiations and movements in international oil prices.

 Brent crude drops 15.9pc as geopolitical tensions ease; market optimism grows despite widening trade deficit

On the macroeconomic front, inflation, measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), slowed to 9.61pc year-on-year in October, down from 10.26pc in September, although it remained significantly higher than 6.25pc recorded in October last year. Average inflation during the first four months of FY27 stood at 10.1pc, compared with 4.7pc in the corresponding period last year.

The government raised around Rs386-400 billion through its latest Pakistan Investment Bonds (PIBs) auction against a target of Rs350bn. Cut-off yields declined by 10-12 basis points across selected tenors, with the strongest participation recorded in three-year bonds, which attracted approximately Rs165.3bn.

The improvement in yields reflected expectations of easing inflationary pressures and a potentially more accommodative monetary policy outlook.

Meanwhile, Pakistan’s trade deficit widened by 20pc year-on-year and 10pc month-on-month to $3.9bn in October, according to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics. Exports increased 2.8pc year-on-year to $2.9bn, while imports rose 11.8pc to $6.8bn, highlighting continued pressure from the import bill.

On the external front, the State Bank of Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves increased by $40 million week-on-week to $21.6bn as of Oct 30, providing import cover of approximately three months. The rupee also edged up 0.03pc against the dollar to close at Rs276.66.

Domestic petroleum prices provided further relief, with petrol prices falling 6.7pc to Rs352.59 per litre and high-speed diesel (HSD) declining 4.6pc to Rs382.25 per litre, following a reduction in ex-refinery prices.

Sectoral data presented a mixed picture. Urea sales surged 39pc year-on-year to 487,000 tonnes in October, led by Fauji Fertiliser Company, whose sales increased 54pc to 257,000 tonnes. Fatima Fertiliser recorded growth of 30pc, while Engro Fertilisers posted a 13pc increase, according to AHL.

Oil production rebounded 8.9pc week-on-week to 64,700 barrels per day, mainly because of the restoration of output from northern fields. Gas production, however, edged down 0.4pc to 3,063 million cubic feet per day.

Refinery throughput increased 9.7pc year-on-year to 1.119 million tonnes in October, supported by higher HSD and furnace oil sales. 

Cement despatches increased 0.4pc year-on-year to 4.8m tonnes, with domestic demand supported by recovering construction activity. Exports remained under pressure amid the continued closure of the Afghan border.

Banking stocks emerged as the biggest contributors to the market’s advance, adding 2,659 points, followed by cement with 1,266 points and fertiliser with 988 points. Power and investment banking shares contributed another 545 and 535 points, respectively.

Among individual stocks, Fauji Fertiliser Company added 613 points, Lucky Cement 564 points, Engro Holdings 519 points, United Bank 491 points and Meezan Bank 480 points. Refinery stocks were the principal drag, with ATRL shedding 163 points and Cnergyico contributing a negative 76 points.

Average daily trading volume increased 43pc week-on-week to 856 million shares, while average traded value rose 24pc to $103m, according to AHL.

Looking ahead, analysts expect market sentiment to remain linked to progress in Middle East diplomacy, international oil prices and domestic economic indicators. Investors will also monitor the MSCI review scheduled for November 11.

AKD Securities believes improving economic fundamentals and any further de-escalation in the Middle East could support equities by lowering oil prices and creating room for monetary easing.

Despite the recent rally, valuations remain relatively attractive. The benchmark index is trading at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of around 7.3 times, with a dividend yield of 6.8pc, while its forward price-to-earnings multiple stands at 6.3 times, according to brokerage estimates.

President Donald Trump's Justice Department is stepping in to rescue a long-running MAGA legal crusade red-state voters just rejected at the ballot box.

The Justice Department told a court Friday night it intends to intervene in a five-year-old Texas lawsuit accusing Planned Parenthood of Medicaid fraud, The New York Times reported Saturday.

The case was a pet project of outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who lost his U.S. Senate bid this week. The Republican running to succeed him as attorney general lost, too. An anonymous plaintiff filed the suit in 2021, and Paxton joined it on the state's behalf the following year.

The suit claims Planned Parenthood's Texas clinic operators and its national federation improperly collected Medicaid reimbursements while the state was working to kick the group out of the program. Planned Parenthood denies the allegations and points out that no court barred it from receiving payments while the fight played out.

Texas wants roughly $1.8 billion in reimbursements, interest and penalties. Planned Parenthood, which recently reported about $2.1 billion in annual revenue, has warned that a payout that large could shut it down.

The move signals the administration may be prepared to undercut Democrats who just won state offices in former GOP strongholds, according to the Times, which noted that Biden's Justice Department passed on joining the case in 2021.

A surprise Democratic sweep in Texas this week handed the attorney general’s office to Nathan Johnson, a veteran litigator who takes office in January. Johnson told the Times he plans to review every lawsuit Paxton filed during his 12-year tenure, and that the review will include this case.

"We are reviewing this action closely, including what it means for Texans and what the law allows," Johnson said in a statement. "When I take office as Attorney General, I will take appropriate action in the interests of my state." He has already vowed to end Paxton's practice of suing out-of-state doctors who mail abortion pills into Texas.

A Planned Parenthood lawyer told the Times the intervention shows Trump is "undeterred by the election results."

"This is an effort by the Trump administration to shut us down," said Susan Baker Manning, general counsel for Planned Parenthood Federation of America. "It is going to weaponize the Department of Justice against us."

Norm Eisen, who served as White House ethics counsel under President Barack Obama and founded the legal advocacy group Democracy Defenders Action, said it's unusual for the Justice Department to jump into a case it had previously declined to join.

"Texas voters have now rejected Paxton and his brand of politicized litigation, which is the Justice Department's only apparent reason for intervening," Eisen said.

The case could head to trial as soon as next spring. The presiding judge, Matthew Kacsmaryk, is a Trump appointee who opposes abortion.

The Texas attorney general's office and the Justice Department did not respond to the Times' requests for comment.
