news.title: Apology and Reparation for Slave Trade: Beyond the Politics of Britain’s Kemi Badenoch
news.text:
Bola A. Akinterinwa

International relations, classical or contemporary, has always been fraught with injustice and unfairness in its conduct and management. The story of the slave trade is a case in point. More than twelve million African people, including men, women, and children, were captured and trafficked to the Americas forcefully as slaves in between the 15th and 19th Centuries. The abduction and trafficking was cruel as an act. When compensations were to be paid at the end of the slave trading, the act was an open manifestation of unfairness and injustice. Slave owners were compensated but the slaves were never considered as qualified to be compensated. This is why the quest for apology and reparation cannot be well appreciated if the nature of slave trading is not first explicated. 

In the words of the UN Secretary General, Antonio Guterres, the wealth of several Western nations of today was largely ‘built on stolen lives and stolen labour…barbaric punishments that maintained control – from shackles and iron collars to flogging and sexual violence.’ The situation ‘was not simply forced labour.’ And perhaps most disturbingly, ‘it was a machinery of mass exploitation and deliberate dehumanization of men, women and children. The wounds run deep and often go unrecognized.’ If this was the situation, why have there not been agitations for apology and reparations before now? How do we explain the fact that international eyes have been closed to the atrocities?

Without whiff of doubt, there are two schools of thought that explain the issue. One school has it that Africa should now be more forward-looking rather than wasting much time on the problems of the past. The other school posits that there cannot be any future without the past and the present defining it. This argument is strengthened by the consideration that Africa and black people are generally portrayed as backward, whereas, it is mainly the factor of slave trading and colonization that also largely explains the backwardness. 

Politics of Reparation for Slave Trade 

Chief Obafemi Awolowo, in his press statement of 28th June, 1961 issued on behalf of the Action Group, already expatiated on the backwardness of the black man that “African Unity is a Necessity,” and that ’from the beginning of recorded history, the black man has been the conspicuous butt of all manner of inhuman treatment. In the palaces of the Arabian potentates – both in the Middle East and in North Africa – he was degraded and enslaved. When the so-called “dark Continent of Africa” was discovered, the European marauders hunted him down like a common beast, captured him, and sold him into slavery in the Americas and West indies.’ 

The enslavement has continued to change in form and Chief Awolowo did not fail to remind us again that ‘the era of trading in, and of enforcing the services of black slaves, was terminated only to be replaced by the European Powers which initiated it with a legalized form of political and economic enslavement of the entire black peoples of the continent of Africa… Today, for most parts of black Africa, the inhumane, humiliating and degrading position delineated above remains more or less the same.’ It was against this background that the struggle against the indignity arising from the enslavement became a desideratum to be addressed.

It was a Nigerian by ius sanguinis, Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola, a President of Nigeria that Nigerians never had, that kick-started the reparation struggle. He single-handedly spearheaded and institutionalized the global and Pan African movement for reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and colonialism in the early 1990s. He explained the need for reparation as restoration of Africa from historical damage caused by slavery and colonization. In between 1987 and 1990, he built special linkages and ties with the African Diaspora in the United States, an effort that was much appreciated and that prompted giving the Congressional Black Caucus Chairman’s Award to him.

And perhaps more interestingly, Chief Abiola, not only financed, but also hosted the foundational Lagos Reparations Conference, generally referred to as the World Conference on Reparations to Africa and Africans in the Diaspora, held on December 13-14, 1990 at the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs, Lagos. The outcome of the Conference served as a catalyst in the adoption of an OAU resolution in 1991 that recognised Africa’s right to redress. In fact, Chief Abiola chaired the OAU Group of Eminent Persons on Reparations and helped to organize the 1993 Abuja Pan-African Conference that formed the International Committee for Reparation. This is the genesis of the current politics of reparation. 

Even if Nigeria has always been the leader of leaders in the quest to defend African interests and integrity, other initiatives had also been taken especially in light of the demise of Chief M.K.O. Abiola and non-follow up to his struggle for reparation. The increasing threats of modern neocolonialism have prompted agitations to put an end to any form of recolonization. True, neocolonialism is making a nonsense of the sovereignty of many African states. At the 19-20 December 2025 Russia-Africa Partnership Forum held in Cairo, Egypt, decisions were taken to stop the ongoing exploitation of Africa and unlock its resources for integration and development. One of the decisions was the need to struggle for reparation for the enslavement of African and black people in the Americas. In fact, African leaders declared 2025 the ‘Year of Reparations.’ It is therefore not a surprise that the issue would be taken more seriously at the level of the UNGA.

On March 25, 2026, which coincided with the International Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Slavery and the Transatlantic Slave Trade, a UN resolution adopted at the 80th session of the UNGA, recognized the transatlantic slavery as the ‘gravest crime against humanity.’ The resolution requested the UN Member States to contribute to a reparations fund. At the UNGA vote on it, 123 countries voted in favour, 52 countries abstained from voting (essentially European Union Member States and the United Kingdom), while 3 countries (United States, Israel, and Argentina) voted against the declaration of the transatlantic slave trade as a crime against humanity.

In June 2026, Yvette Tan of the BBC had it that ‘African and Caribbean nations called for formal apology for transatlantic slavery… A 19-point reparations plan has been endorsed as part of the “Next Steps” conference in the Ghanaian capital, Accra’ (www.bbc.com). The reparation request includes a comprehensive debt relief, the restitution of looted cultural property, and the establishment of a global reparations fund. More important, the conference leaders wanted all the countries involved in the slave trade to offer their ‘full, formal and unconditional apologies.’ One rationale for this position is the belief of the Ghanaian president, John Dramani Mahama that ‘history does not ask us to inherit guilt, but it asks us to inherit responsibility’ (ibid.). It is this question of responsibility that is being politicized internationally.

From the perspective of the Americans, the United States does not ‘recognise a legal right to reparations for historical wrongs that were not illegal under international law at the time they occurred.’ Explained differently, there are three main issues raised in the position of the United States. First, slave trading as at the time it occurred was legal; Secondly, the United States admits that slave trade was a historical wrong but it cannot be an issue for reparation, and thirdly, in the event it is seen as a right, the United States does not recognize such a right. More concernedly, the United States argued that the UN resolution is not specific on ‘whom the recipients of reparatory justice would be.’ 

China is in support of the UN resolution declaring the transatlantic slave trade as the ‘gravest crime against humanity’ and that the slave trade left centuries-long structural and developmental wounds on the African continent. As told by Chinese Plenipotentiary to Nigeria, Yu Dunhai, the resolution is a historic milestone and a victory for justice: ‘justice may be delayed, but it will never be absent… With profound historical significance it represents a powerful affirmation of historical justice, a firm defence of the common dignity of humanity, and a major victory for the international community in opposing the remnants of colonialism, resisting racial discrimination, and upholding fairness and justice. 

Russia supports the UNGA resolution and promised in January 2026 to assist Africa to scientifically and mathematically calculate and quantify claims for Western colonial and slave trade reparations. In the words of the Director of the Institute for African Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Irina Abramova, ‘we want to combine the efforts of Russian scientists – mathematicians, programmers, historians and economists – with African scientists in order to jointly substantiate the volume of these reparations and then proceed with legal claims on various international platforms.’ Director Abramova advised Africa to seek exact mathematical reparation to be paid by the Western colonialist and slave traders and the potential recipients of the reparation funds.

Latin America, with the exception of Argentina, supports the UNGA resolution. Agitation for reparation in Brazil, which was the last country to abolish slavery in 1888 and which accounted for about 5 million out of the 12.5 million forcibly-trafficked slaves to the Americas, is tied to land reform. All the EU Member States abstained from the UNGA resolution in the belief that claims for historical compensation are inconsistent with international law in the sense that slavery was legal under the laws of the time. Unlike the transatlantic system, there are no official state-level reparations programmes or formal financial compensations from Arab or Middle Eastern governments to sub-Sahara Africa. This is an overview of great power politics of slave trade reparation.

Beyond Kemi Badenoch’s Non-apology 

Kemi Badenoch is against the idea of apologizing for four main reason. First, it would be a ‘navel-gazing distraction’ in her own words. A navel-gazing distraction is the ‘practice or habit of spending too much time absorbed in deep, self-indulgent, or unproductive contemplation of (one’s) own thoughts, feelings, problems, or ego.’ In other words, Badenoch is actually saying that, rather than the British people expending an excessive, self-indulgent and unproductive amount of time on their own problems, feelings and thoughts, the British should pay useful attention to the outside world.

As good as this thinking may be, it is still meaningless because, if the British refuse to first internalize the implications of not paying reparation, engaging with the external world may be more costly and problematic. Badenoch wants the British to be less excessive in self-contemplation. The principle of reparation in international law stipulates that a state responsible for an internationally-wrongful act or a violation of human rights has a legal obligation to make full reparation for the injury caused. The opponents of non-reparation argue that slave trading was lawful as at the time it took place. The proponents of slave trading reparation are not talking about slave trade as a business, but as an act of brutalities, indecency, that condones wickedness and inhumanity.

The modern-day British and Americans wrongly argue that they should not be held for the crimes of slave trading committed by their fore parents. What their fore parents did then was precisely still impacting on the conduct and management of international politics today. In fact, the defence and sustainability of the basic principles and guidelines on the right to a remedy and reparation for victims of gross violations of International Human Rights Law and Serious Violations of International Humanitarian Law largely depends on the extent of fairness and justice in the management of global affairs. 

Secondly, Kemi Badenoch has queried the usefulness of future leaders attending the Commonwealth summit in light of the increasing calls for reparation. Good query, but the unending demands for reparation are compelling reasons to see the beauty in navel-gazing distraction. The truth still in the making is that, sooner than later, the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) has the potential to witness a decline in its influence, if any attempt is made to return the Commonwealth of Nations to its former status of British Commonwealth. Doing so could precipitate the disintegration of the organization.

Thirdly, there is the permissible reparation offered by the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, who said there would not be reparations in the form of financial compensation and that, in lieu, he is prepared to engage in helping poorer countries to restructure their debts on more favourable terms. This seems to be another way of saying NO to the payment of reparation. A debt is necessarily an obligation and a relationship between a debtor and a creditor. Regardless of the type or nature of a debt – secured debt which is backed by collateral; unsecured debts; installment debt, which is a fixed lump sum repaid in regular scheduled payment over a set time; and revolving debt – the truth is that none of the common payoff strategies puts an end to the indebtedness. Debts must still be paid. 

Put differently, common payoff strategies are of three types. First is debt avalanche, which involves paying the debt with the highest interest rate first in order to save money on total interests. The second is debt snowball approach, which is about paying off the smallest balance first to build psychological momentum. The third is the consolidation approach, which is combining multiple high-interest debts into a single, lower-interest. All these payoff strategies still require payment of debts. 

Since reparation is, stricto sensu, not a loan but a relationship in which a misunderstanding is resolved, Prime Minister Burnham’s offer of facilitating restructuring of Africa’s debts cannot be good enough for negotiation. What is advisable and be good enough is outright cancellation of all debts, London, and Paris, Club inclusive. Interests already paid are more than the capital loans taken. Even if we talk about the grant of development aid, the giver of the aid has generally been the first beneficiary of the implementation of its own aid policy.

Fourthly, and perhaps more interestingly, Kemi Badenoch appeared to be much inspired by an earlier statement made 20 years ago by Tony Blair, who said ‘the Commonwealth should be looking forward, not endlessly backward.’ True, this is a good point of observation. However, when talking about the ‘past endlessly’ or ‘endlessly backward,’ and no one is listening, is the solution the need to stop looking backward? It cannot. One ideal solution is to continue to sustain looking backward until those affected will not only listen but will also make their future generations learn lessons of humanity from the saga. Besides, it is very difficult, if not impossible, to seek to obliterate the indignities of the past by sustaining them in different forms today and at the same time preaching the sermons of forgetting the past. There is no today without yesterday, nor will there be any tomorrow without today and without today being reckoned with as part of the continuum of history.

While we agree with Kemi Badenoch on the ‘need to start looking at how we can bring the Commonwealth together, start looking forward, not backward,’ our agreement does not include rejection of discussions on payment of reparations. It is a critical issue in maintaining a balance within the Commonwealth organization. 

Andy Burnham is against financial reparation. Fine it is. Reparation may not be financial. Africa is not crazy about financial reparation. In Brazil, for example, no one is talking about financial reparation. Reparation in Brazil centres on land reform and its challenges. In the context of Africa, let justice and fairness in the management of global questions be the case in the slave trade reparation struggle. The Honourable Conservative party leader should simply note that the struggle for slave trade reparation is unconsciously and gradually becoming more of a people’s movement. Apology has become a desideratum in order to maintain global peace and security. Global governance must be driven by rule of law and not by policies of unilateralism which have been condoned for too long. The emergence of the BRICS ought to have sent good lessons to the sponsors of realist school of thought that power can no longer alone solve the problems of humanity. Therefore, Badenoch should begin to exercise more caution concerning Andy Burnham’s navel-gazing distraction.

Badenoch should not be in a hurry to forget that the management of the United States under President Donald Trump, or the implementation of the policy of ‘Make America Great Again’ has seriously damaged whatever influence the United States may want to claim to have in Africa. The United Kingdom and the United States have generally acted pari passu in the abuse of the international rule of law. Under the watch of the British, naked aggression has become an acceptable tradition. Imagine how the United States’ unilateral abduction of Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela, a sovereign state, with his wife, at dead midnight. Imagine the United States also threatening another sovereign state, Iran, that it would wipe it out of global map. Arrogance of power must be better managed. Who really is interested in this type of kangaroo governance under the pretext of national security? Is it not because there are followers that there are leaders and that leadership has meaning? 

The various western institutions that have been dominating international businesses have the potential to be seriously undermined if the way the developed world is going about the exercise of its strength is not redefined. Africa should be specially respected because of its poverty. Africa’s poverty is the main instrument for the wealth of Europe. If Europe wants to have peace and rest of mind, efforts should be honestly made to address the injustice that has come to characterize the management of international relations. The issue of slave trade reparation and cancellation of Africa’s debts should be addressed more seriously.

In this regard, Kemi Badenoch belief that Britain should not apologise for the UN-identified ‘gravest crime against humanity’ is uncalled for, most unfortunate, unreasonable and myopic. Historical records have shown that slaves were flogged to death. They were not treated as human beings but as material property. Several maltreated slaves died during transportation from Africa to the Americas and were simply dumped into the high seas for fishes to eat. The statement of Chief Obafemi Awolowo on the brutalities of the slave trade is quite touching. Imagine, the British and Americans argue that these brutalities were lawful during the period of the slave trading. If they were lawful, it meant that there was nothing like humanity the way it exists today. Were the slave masters of that time better than wild animals, if the law they made enabled the payment of reparation to slave masters for losing their properties, who were human beings but who were treated as a chiffon de papier to be thrown into the dustbin of history? Additionally, the Kemi Badenochs of this world are unable to understand that the purpose of the reparation struggle is to restore black dignity. Predictably, the world of the foreseeable future is that of the Black people. Technological expertise will not be the exclusive preserve of the developed world. Veto power will be in désuétude. Sovereign equality will have a more constructive meaning. All the black people claiming to be white will soon learn that acquisition of nationality by ius soli, naturalisation, marriage, conferment, etc., does not really make them a fully blooded American, a French or British, Russian, or Canadian, etc. At best, they will be second class citizens even if the law provides for the contrary. Consequently, let a black man learn how to be black. Not learning so will make them suffer unending indignities. Let Badenoch’s politics anticipate these challenges.

news.title: Supreme Court justice sounds the alarm on ‘crazy’ rulings from her own bench: report
news.text:
A Supreme Court justice offered a blunt assessment of her own court's recent work this weekend, and she suggested she wasn't kidding.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor said she hopes the high court will "take back some of the crazy things that it's done," Politico reported Saturday. The Obama appointee quickly added that she was only joking before reversing herself with "maybe not."

She made the remarks during an hourlong appearance at George Washington's Mount Vernon estate in Virginia, where a conference was examining the past and future of American democracy. Sotomayor told the audience the country is going through a "rough patch" on the rule of law and civic discourse.

"I think we're in a rough patch right now. There's so many challenges to it on so many different levels. This is a really critical point in our history," she said.

Sotomayor singled out one ruling she would like to see reversed, which was the 2024 decision holding that President Donald Trump could not be prosecuted for many acts tied to his official duties. She and the court's two other liberal justices dissented.

"There are some opinions that I hope in my lifetime will get overturned. The immunity case is one of them," she said.

She also said she feels for teachers, especially those covering constitutional law, given what she called "systemic changes in my court's jurisprudence."

Sotomayor suggested lawmakers may need to step in to restore eroded norms, though she offered no specifics.

"We will come out of this changed and there are some norms that we may have lost forever, but I don't think we will fail as a democracy," she said.

She also blamed a breakdown in civility for weakening civic life. "That someone disagrees with you doesn't make them a bad person, and that's something we've forgotten," she said.

Sotomayor steered clear of commenting directly on this week's midterm results but called Tuesday's "outpouring of voters" an encouraging sign. Turnout landed near 49 percent, a level topped in modern midterms only in 2018, according to Politico.

Still, she voiced confidence the country will recover. "I'm hoping it's...in my lifetime. But even if it's not in my lifetime, I genuinely believe it will happen," she said.

news.title: Trump Makes Wild Election Claim as Miller Takes the Reins
news.text:
Donald Trump is declaring victory in an election that hasn’t been decided—and using his own version of election math to do it.

In a remarkably bold Truth Social post Saturday afternoon, the president, 80, insisted that Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan was “leading substantially” in Alaska’s razor-thin Senate race—even though Democrat Mary Peltola is ahead in the vote count. 

Trump’s reasoning? Votes cast for two other candidates should simply be added to Sullivan’s total.

“Daniel Sullivan is leading substantially in the Alaska Senatorial Race. When you add Daniel (3,600, 1.68%) into Dan, and Gerald Heikes (4,846, 2.27%), Senator Dan Sullivan is up by thousands of Votes,” Trump began. 

Peltola leads with 48.17 percent of the vote, while (Trump’s preferred) Sullivan trails by fewer than 700 votes, with 47.88 percent.

Only 75 percent of ballots have been counted so far. Under Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system, if no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote, the lowest-ranked candidates are eliminated and their votes redistributed according to voters’ next preferences.

Trump’s math ignores that crucial distinction. Votes don’t automatically transfer to whichever candidate the president believes should receive them, and some may not transfer to either major-party candidate at all.

The race may not be decided until Nov. 18, when Alaska is scheduled to conduct its ranked-choice vote tabulation.

That’s not soon enough for Trump, who has been laser-focused on alleged “voter fraud” in Alaska since before Election Day.

Another Dan Sullivan ran in both the primary and general elections, and his candidacy appears to have served as a spoiler. His candidacy faced repeated legal challenges, but courts and election officials consistently ruled that he could remain on the ballot. 

Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. is currently in fourth place with just 1.68 percent of the vote, well behind Dan S. Sullivan, who was identified on the ballot as the Republican incumbent.

Trump’s post came just 24 hours after the president announced Stephen Miller’s elevation to White House chief of staff. And Miller has already weighed in on the Alaska race, describing it as “one of the most egregious attacks we have seen on the integrity of American elections.”

Miller, who was questioned by the House committee investigating the Jan. 6 Capitol attack about his role in encouraging the “Stop the Steal” movement, drafted part of the speech Trump delivered at the Ellipse before rioters stormed the Capitol.

Miller also argued on X last month that the Sullivan-versus-Sullivan debacle “reveals pure contempt for voters” and laid the blame on Democrats.

Four days after Miller’s post, The New York Times reported allegations that Peltola’s campaign may have coordinated with Daniel J. Sullivan to get him on the ballot.

Peltola’s campaign has denied the allegation.

Trump’s Saturday post also claimed that the independent candidate, Heikes, was fraudulent, without providing evidence, and declared the race “OVER.”

“I don’t know what takes so long to announce his win. This should be immediate! Anyone voting for Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., a man who tried to change his middle initial, but was unable to get it done in time, and who was otherwise nonpolitical – Never even voted – is a vote for Senator Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Race is OVER. Dan Sullivan WON, BY A LOT!”

It wasn’t Trump’s first such demand this week as he licks his wounds following decisive Democratic victories in the midterms.

On Thursday, he threw a similar tantrum on Truth Social, claiming that reallocating the independent candidate’s votes to Sen. Sullivan was the only solution.

“There is no other fair solution!” he opined. 

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

news.text:

Update: Dana White has since declined, according to a CNN report.— ESPN (@espn) November 7, 2026

White was at a boxing event Saturday that was being hosted in London. A UFC spokesperson didn’t respond after being requested for comment.

The boss of UFC posted an image on Instagram of the president’s post, doing so with a photo of himself behind the White House press briefing room podium that read, “On to the next chapter.”

The post from Trump comes as the White House deals with a transitional period and the Republican Party’s massive defeat in the midterm elections Tuesday.

Historical victories by candidates in the Democratic Party, which include areas that the GOP controlled for decades, resulted in the Republicans losing both the Senate and House of Representatives.

Indian Americans showed discontent towards Republican policies mainly driven by immigration and economic issues

Washington: Indian Americans voted against the Republicans largely due to anger against the policies pursued by the Trump administration and not on the issue of foreign policy or the US attitude towards India, said Sumitra Badrinathan, who closely studies voting patterns in the US.In an interview with PTI, Badrinathan said despite the challenging environment due to President Donald Trump's immigration policies, Indian Americans still find the US better suited for pursuing studies and careers than European countries."We've consistently asked Indian Americans whether they care about their politicians' stance towards India, and the answer always seems to be a 'no'," said Badrinathan, assistant professor of Political Sciences at American University.Badrinathan, along with Milan Vaishnav, Director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, and others, released the Indian American Attitudes Survey aimed at understanding how the Indian diaspora approaches electoral politics in the US.In the recently concluded midterm elections, six Indian American candidates were elected to the US House of Representatives, while over 30 won seats in state legislatures and other public offices.Live EventsRepublican Vivek Ramaswamy lost a bitterly contested election for the post of Governor of Ohio, his home state and that of Vice President J D Vance.Republicans lost control of the US Congress to Democrats, turning Trump into a lame duck president in the final two years of his tenure.Trump acknowledged that his party lost the elections due to anger among the people facing high inflation caused by the Iran war.However, Badrinathan argued that blaming just inflation and high oil prices for the Republican loss would be oversimplistic."We found that the issues that motivate Indian Americans are actually the same issues that motivate general Americans. They talk about jobs, the economy, cost of living. It's possible that this time, H-1B, discrimination, and those sorts of issues played a slightly larger role," she said.Anti-India sentiment dominated the election campaign in Texas, the state with the second-highest Indian-American population in the US, and remarks by Republican leader Bo French targeting University of Texas students triggered widespread outrage cutting across party lines."It's hard to say if the Bo French tweet alone pushed people to vote a certain way, as opposed to what came with it: changes around actual immigration policies, the rhetoric around it, and changes in the economy making people's lives harder. So, yes, it probably played a part," Badrinathan said.She said Indian Americans on average tend to have a pretty negative view of specific Trump policies around immigration, tariffs and H-1B visas.Badrinathan refused to hazard a guess on the policies Democrats are likely to pursue towards India now that they have control of both the US House and the Senate."It's a new dawn. It's really hard to say whether the majority that the Democrats now hold in the House and Senate as well as multiple state legislatures is going to translate to policy or whether it's going to lead to gridlock," she said."It's also hard to say whether the discourse is going to change because establishment Democrats have now seemingly taken a little bit of a backseat to let in some space for newcomers across states," she said, referring to the number of Democratic Socialists of America candidates emerging victorious in the midterm elections.Badrinathan said despite the tough immigration policies and discrimination against Indians, the interest in studying in the US continues to remain high."But it seems like even despite the perception that there is discrimination and one in two people saying they do experience some form of discrimination, mostly on the basis of skin colour, exit from the US is not happening. People are still encouraged to come to the US to both work and to study," Badrinathan said.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: MAGA senator’s comeback now a ‘mathematical impossibility’: legal expert
news.text:
An election lawyer fresh from a deep-red state's ballot count says one embattled MAGA senator has hit a dead end.

Norm Eisen, the former White House ethics czar who served as counsel to House Democrats during President Donald Trump's first impeachment, told progressive commentator Brian Tyler Cohen in a Saturday episode of his YouTube show that Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-MS) has no realistic path left to beat Democratic challenger Scott Colom. "It's a mathematical impossibility at this point for Senator Hyde-Smith," Eisen said.

Eisen, who said he spent three days in Mississippi and planned to head back the next day, pegged Colom's lead as "approaching a 3,000-vote margin." He compared the count to the 2000 Florida recount he worked on, when the gap bounced around in the hundreds.

"We're well out of that space now, and it's really moved out of the margin of contestation," he said.

The race has not been called. Straight Arrow News reported that Colom, a district attorney, was ahead by just over 1,000 votes as of Thursday. The outlet noted that Mississippi has no automatic recount, so a losing candidate would have to go to court after certification. A Colom win would hand Mississippi its first Democratic senator since 1982 and its first Black senator since Reconstruction, the outlet reported.

Eisen flagged what he called "two concerning episodes" from Republicans. One was a letter he described as "full of misrepresentations." It asked for affidavit ballots, Mississippi's version of provisional ballots, to be handled differently.

"You open the affidavit ballot, if the address matches, it's approved for the count. That's Mississippi law," Eisen said.

The other was a press conference where a former U.S. attorney representing Republicans hinted at a challenge without committing to one.

"They got the losing hand," Eisen said. "When it's big like that, you know you're going to lose. Do you really want to go on a kamikaze mission?"

Eisen laid out the remaining deadlines. Voters who lacked photo ID have until 5 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 10, to show it at their circuit court. Counties certify Nov. 13, and the state must declare results by Dec. 3.

The county certification date is "likely when you're going to get the AP call and the networks will call the race for Scott," Eisen predicted.

He also tore into Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson, a Republican. "The worst thing he did this year was purge the voter list," Eisen said, adding, "That's why we have these affidavit ballots."

Eisen credited a string of legal wins against Trump. He said that after his side "knocked the stuffing legally out of Donald Trump at the Supreme Court on Monday night, he gave up the sabotage and he was wiped out by the blue wave."
